#989. England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or

The England captain ends his country's 25-year wait for the prestigious award after scoring 73 goals for club and country last season, beating competition from Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe.

England captain Harry Kane won the men's Ballon d'Or for the first time on Monday, becoming the first English player to receive the prestigious football award since 2001.

The 33-year-old Bayern Munich striker was honored at a ceremony at the London Palladium after scoring 73 goals in 65 appearances for club and country last season.

The Ballon d'Or, awarded by French magazine France Football, is one of football's most prestigious individual honors, recognizing the world's best players.

The last English player to win the award was former Liverpool striker Michael Owen, who claimed the prize 25 years ago.

Kane's remarkable goalscoring record helped Bayern Munich secure a German league and cup double last season.

The former Tottenham Hotspur forward also led England to the World Cup semifinals, the country's best finish since winning the tournament in 1966.

Kane has finished as the Bundesliga's leading scorer for three consecutive seasons. He was also Europe's top club goalscorer during the 2025-26 campaign.

At Monday's ceremony, Kane thanked his Bayern Munich teammates for their support.

"Without you guys (his Bayern Munich team-mates) and the rest of the team it wouldn't be possible, the way you guys push me, the way we compete. So thank you very much," he said.

Kane also paid tribute to his former club Tottenham Hotspur, which he joined at the age of 11, as well as his England teammates and family.

"To my wife Kate, my best friend. We've been through ups and downs. You are my biggest support and I felt like you wanted this more than me," he said.

Reflecting on his career, Kane encouraged young footballers to pursue their ambitions despite setbacks.

"I hope my journey, it wasn't straightforward, I didn't go straight to the top, I had to experience a lot of loan moves and fight my way to get to where I am now. I hope that can give you inspiration."

Kane faced strong competition from Barcelona's Spanish teenager Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid's French forward Kylian Mbappe.

He joins Stanley Matthews, Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen among the English players to have won the award.

Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas claimed the women's Ballon d'Or for the third time in her career, having previously won the award in 2021 and 2022.

The 32-year-old was recognized after a successful season with Barcelona, winning the treble and scoring 21 goals across all competitions.

Putellas also played a key role in Barcelona's Champions League triumph, contributing seven goals and seven assists during the campaign.

She joined English club London City Lionesses in July after spending 14 years at Barcelona.

Her victory ended a run of three consecutive Ballon d'Or wins by fellow Spaniard Aitana Bonmatí.

Barcelona's Lamine Yamal won the Kopa Trophy for the best young male player for the third consecutive year, while his teammate Vicky Lopez claimed the women's award for the second year running.

Barcelona coach Pere Romeu was named women's coach of the year, while Spain manager Luis de la Fuente won the men's coaching award.

Spain goalkeeper Unai Simon received the men's Yashin Trophy, with Cata Coll winning the women's equivalent.

Barcelona was named women's club of the year, while Paris Saint-Germain took the men's award.

#988. Football Daily | Aston Villa, ‘unacceptable insults’ and thin-skinned clutching of pearls

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

When Jamie Carragher appeared as a pundit on Sky Sports Super Sunday, Football Daily was surprised he didn’t have a solicitor sitting alongside him, occasionally jotting notes on a pad or leaning over to give whispered instructions and answer “no comment” to any leading questions about Trey Nyoni starting ahead of Ryan Gravenberch. On Friday night, the former Liverpool defender was subjected to a threat of legal action from Aston Villa, who took such grave exception to some “unacceptable insults” he had rained down on them from his podcast pulpit, that they were ready to call in the heavy legal artillery and stop him from preventing their “ascension in English and European football”. Taking a leaf out of the tried-and-much-ridiculed Nottingham Forest playbook, Villa chair Nassef Sawiris appears to have eschewed contacting Carragher through the usual formal channels and instead cajoled some unfortunate junior comms staffer to make the portentous announcement on their Social Media Disgraces.

Villa’s threat came on the back of some fairly obvious observations he made on Stick To Football, when he pointed out that English football has a food-chain and despite their commendable successes in recent seasons, Villa aren’t quite as high up it as the richest man in Egypt might like to think. During a debate about the likelihood of Unai Emery leaving Villa to take over the soon-to-be-vacant head coach’s job at Manchester United, Carragher had said the Spaniard would “want that opportunity to manage a giant again”, before pointing out “there is a chain in football, whether you like it or not”. As controversial footballing takes go, it was right up there with pointing out that bears defecate in the woods and Pope Leo XIV wears a funny hat. “So shut the [eff] up Aston Villa fans,” honked Carragher, hitting his stride. “Aston Villa will never be Manchester United.”

Of course, with this being football, there is always a danger that explicitly signposted and totally anodyne badinage will inevitably be misinterpreted by thin-skinned folk who are desperate to be offended. But it is usually self-professed terminally-online superfans, not multi-billionaire club chairs whose hands instinctively reach for their pearls. While it remains unclear what exactly it was he said that was actionable, Carragher subsequently apologised for his comments. “I’d like to apologise to Aston Villa, the owners & their fans,” he trumpeted from his soapbox in the digital town square. “My language this week was clumsy & wrong. I can assure Villa fans it was tongue in cheek but I can understand it’s not come across that way, so apologies. Good luck today UTV!”

It has now been reported that Villa have dropped their threat of unspecified legal action against Carragher but it remains to be seen if Fulham can look forward to hearing from their lawyers after helping to prevent their ascension up the league after [Snip! Snip! Snippety-snip! – Football Daily Lawyers] at Villa Park on Saturday night.

#986. Barry leads Everton comeback win vs Coventry - who suffer triple VAR woe

Everton vs Coventry City. Premier League.

Report and free highlights as Everton beat Coventry 3-1; Frank Lampard's side had two penalties waved away by VAR either side of half-time, including one for a James Tarkowski hair pull; Yann Gboho put Coventry ahead, but Thierno Barry scored two and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall made it 3-1

Football Journalist @SamBIitz

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Thierno Barry continued his fine form as his two goals and an assist fired Everton to a comeback 3-1 win over Coventry - who had three big VAR calls go against them on Merseyside.

Everton's only available striker scored his ninth and 10th goals of the season in similar fashion - nodding in two headers at the back post after Yann Gboho had given Coventry the lead at the start of an epic second half.

But that was only one part of the story, as officiating controversy dominated the game. In the first half, James Tarkowski avoided punishment for an apparent hair pull on Caleb Yirenkyi in the penalty box.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

VAR Tim Wood checked and cleared Tarkowski's challenge on the Coventry midfielder - and the technology was needed again after half-time.

Taiwo Awoniyi ran through towards the box and went down under Vitalii Mykolenko's challenge. VAR checked the foul and deemed there was contact - but outside the penalty area.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

These two big calls initially didn't matter as Gboho scored his first Coventry goal in fine fashion, slaloming through challenges and poking past Jordan Pickford.

But four minutes later, Barry took over. First, he headed at the back post from Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall's cross before a second, similar goal had more controversy attached.

Barry bundled the winner home amid accusations from Coventry he used his hand in the move. VAR said there was no conclusive angle which showed the Everton forward handled the ball in. VAR Wood said: "Okay, that's [hit] his side, that's definitely not hand. Confirming on-field decision of goal."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Barry then turned provider to seal the result - as his eye-of-the-needle pass released Dewsbury-Hall to fire in from a tight angle. The Everton midfielder responding well to Thomas Tuchel leaving him out of the England squad earlier on Friday.

Coventry remain two points above the relegation zone and could fall into the bottom three come the end of the weekend. Everton have jumped into fifth - leapfrogging rivals Liverpool for 48 hours at least.

Reading on Sky Sports Scores? The Sky Sports app is better than ever - tap to find out why...

Coventry head coach Frank Lampard to Sky Sports:

"The first-half decision on Tarkowski got checked. And seeing it back, he pulls on Caleb's hair while competing with Ethan [Pinnock].

"I thought the rules were clear. I know they've changed the rules so it's no red card, I get that too. But he's pulling on his hair and [Yirenkyi] can't get his momentum to jump, I think it's a foul and a penalty and they decided no.

"I thought the one on Taiwo running through - it's a clear foul that the referee doesn't give in-game. I can't believe that because it's clear. Maybe he waited for VAR because it was on the borderline.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"But as I see it, Taiwo's foot is entering the box and his knee and the back of his knee is on the line of the box, which is a penalty. That goes against us with VAR.

"And then Barry's second goal comes off his hand. I hate to sound like a moaner. It's a football match and if you win the game, that can happen here. I've worked here and know the momentum swings in the game. And I'm not trying to talk about the circumstances of the actual football.

"But when big decisions change games, they absolutely do. It's disappointing. VAR is there for that and it didn't do its job."

On Barry's second goal: "His last touch flicks it in the net. It was a really quick check a well. People may disagree, but it's my opinion."

There was no communication from the Premier League Match Centre on if the hair pull was reviewed in this game, but there was new guidance from the Premier League this summer, which reads: "A red card will be issued when there is a clear and deliberate action to pull an opponent's hair with excessive force and/or brutality.

"A yellow card will be issued if the action is deemed to be without excessive force and/or brutality.

"Referees will enhance recognition of clear holding actions that have a clear material impact, and/or non-footballing holding actions with no place on the football pitch. This includes penalising defenders where they are clearly only focused on opponents and making a holding action that is impactful on the attacker's ability to play or challenge for the ball."

Sky Sports' Jamie Redknapp on Friday Night Football:

"Sometimes you need things to go your way. You need a little bit of luck and there's no doubt they had that today.

"The Yirenkyi one should have been a penalty, the Awoniyi one should have been a penalty - the VAR brushed that aside too quickly as his foot is definitely on the line.

"That could have changed the complexity of the game. But it didn't. And Everton got the points.

"We've looked at [the second Barry goal] forensically and I do think it touches his hand. But when you're asking VAR to intervene and disallow the goal, it's difficult.

"I watched it for maybe five to ten minutes and I've come to the conclusion that I think it was, but I understand why VAR didn't give it because it's not clear and obvious enough

"It brushes his fingers. It's accidental as well, does it mean to hit his hands?

"It does divert it a little bit, but if we're going to get to that point where we're forensically looking at every single thing, it becomes hard. The frustration Frank Lampard will have is inevitable."

"The efforts were good. The performance I didn't think reached the heights we did recently. But getting three points in the Premier League, you take it every way you can. It keeps us near the top end, not the bottom end.

"We had a quick turnaround from Monday to Friday. It's enough days but maybe a bit quick. We didn't perform. But I have to give Coventry credit, they did a lot of good things. You have no divine right to come here and think you're going to beat Coventry. They had opportunities and things could have gone other ways tonight.

"[The Coventry goal] was [the kick up the backside we needed]. We were just playing through and thinking we would eventually get the goal. Thierno gets another couple of goals, Kiernan got another one. It's not a night to be negative about the players, I just know we can play much better than we did tonight.

"I'm bothered because we want it [the result] to be right. But we've had a few decisions recently where we don't think have gone our way. There was one possibly at Newcastle but there was one at Man City last season in a league game which was hugely important for us regarding getting into Europe. That didn't go in our favour. Some times they go for you, something they don't. If they were going against me, I'd be complaining a bit more."

#985. ‘An absolute afterthought’: the story of the Nigeria women’s team’s fall from grace

The Super Falcons won’t be at the World Cup and with the prize money going up, they risk being left even further behind

It was a historic result in Casablanca – but not in a good way. Nigeria’s 2-1 defeat against South Africa in a playoff in August meant that the Super Falcons are missing out on the World Cup for the first time. It is a crushing blow for the most decorated national side in Africa across both men and women, one that has won no fewer than 10 Wafcon titles.

The journalist and lecturer Dr Victor Ademola was in Morocco the day of the defeat. “It was a very difficult evening,” he says. “Some players were visibly emotional while others appeared to be processing what had just happened. I saw players crying as they got on to the team bus while some sat alone or remained on their phones, looking very sad.”

The blow of missing out on the World Cup in Brazil next year came only a few days after they were eliminated from Wafcon at the quarter-final stage by Cameroon – only the semi-finalists qualified for the World Cup automatically, hence Nigeria ending up in that ill-fated playoff.

“What struck me most was the weight of what the result represented,” Ademola says. “These players knew the history of the Super Falcons and understood that this was not simply another defeat. There was a sense of disappointment, disbelief and heartbreak.”

The loss is not only historical but consequential. Nigeria will miss out on developmental funding with next year’s prize fund expected to rise from the previous tournament four years ago. In 2023 the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, pledged to equal the men’s and women’s tournaments prize funds by 2027. The figure for the men’s World Cup in the US, Canada and Mexico was $727m (roughly £539m). Recent news suggest Fifa will miss out on its target but it is nevertheless a blow for Nigeria not to be involved.

Janine Anthony, the African women’s football journalist, says the stakes for the Super Falcons were especially high as “women’s football does not have the luxury of not being at a World Cup”. Anthony adds: “A spot at the World Cup is the ultimate window and it’s a dream to be able to represent your country at any stage, whether it’s in music or football. For women’s football, the World Cup is such a commercially marketable vehicle. The Super Falcons team were one of only seven teams that had been to every World Cup, [and] the only African team. Now that’s gone.”

Anthony says that despite the Super Falcons’ success they are treated as an “absolute afterthought” in terms of the domestic leagues, management and preparation. The lack of preparation games proved problematic in Morocco, she suggests, manifesting itself in a lack of cohesiveness in most games. The then coach, Justine Madugu, frequently changed the starting XI throughout the tournament.

Before the tournament the team played two games against Senegal, who have never qualified for the World Cup, whereas before the 2025 edition they had three friendlies, against France, Cameroon and Portugal. “Imagine if they had more games to prepare,” Anthony says. “Then they could have probably done all the tweaking from a tactical perspective. The Nigerian Football Federation absolutely failed to capitalise on the Wafcon being moved to July.”

The landscape of African women’s football is changing, and Morocco are the only country from the continent who played in the 2023 World Cup who are guaranteed to be at next year’s tournament. South Africa are going into the inter-continental playoffs which start this month, and Nigeria and Zambia are out.

At the Wafcon, Malawi and Cameroon emerged as the standouts. It was Malawi’s debut at the tourmanent and the team gave a stellar performance with the attacking skill of the Chawinga sisters, Tabitha and Temwa, standing out. They will play at their first World Cup. The winners, Cameroon, were unexpected competitors at Wafcon, only qualifying after the Confederation of African Football expanded the tournament from 12 to 16 teams.

The Super Falcons’ absence from the World Cup next year is just the latest setback in a long line of disappointments. The men’s team have failed to qualify for two World Cups in a row while the under-17 men’s team have not reached the World Cup since 2019 or even Afcon since 2023. There have been signs of progress for the the under-20 women, who beat England 3-0 to reach the quarter-finals at their World Cup in September, but they then promptly lost against Colombia 1-0.

Players and coaches have long spoken out and protested against unpaid allowances and bonuses by the Nigerian Football Federation. The Super Falcons have staged numerous sit-ins and training boycotts to protest against the conditions, including at the Wafcons in 2004, 2016 and 2022 as well as the 2019 World Cup.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

The NFF is under investigation by the country’s department of state services for an alleged misuse of a 17bn naira (£9.5m) fund issued by the government in 2024 to address outstanding payments owed to players and staff of the national teams, according to local media. The NFF did not comment when contacted by the Guardian regarding the accusations.

Nigeria’s president, Bola Tinubu, is unhappy about the situation. “Nigerian football must undergo far-reaching changes to strengthen governance, administration, stakeholder representation, player development, domestic competitions and accountability,” he said in August.

That came shortly after Ibrahim Gusau resigned as NFF president along with several other board members. The NFF was scheduled to hold elections in September but they were suspended. They are now expected to take place following reforms made in consultation with Fifa and Caf.

What does the future hold for the Super Falcons? Anthony hopes for more investment, accountability and a bridge between veteran players and the current team on an administration level. “We can only hope that there is the understanding that the Nigerian fans are really disappointed and sad that their national teams aren’t bringing the joy that Nigerians are used to as a football loving nation,” she says. “We can only hope that the Super Falcons can finally be given the respect they’ve always deserved.”

Derby eased the building pressure on boss John Eustace as they hit back to beat Bolton 2-1 in the Championship.

But the change was rapid after the break. Ryan Nyambe poked in his first ever career goal - in his 309th appearance - within 60 seconds of the restart. Jack Robinson then quickly netted to complete the turnaround.

Jesus de Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest after colliding with goalkeeper Jesus Owono - who now could face criminal charges

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Jesus Owono could face prison for his part in the death of Jesus de Miguel, the Tenerife striker who tragically lost his life following a cardiac arrest.

The football world is in mourning for De Miguel after the 30-year-old suffered a cardiac arrest in hospital in Santa Cruz on Tuesday morning, following a high challenge from Andorra FC goalkeeper Owono in a La Liga 2 clash between the two teams.

Owono collided with De Miguel towards the end of the game, with 10-man Andorra chasing the match from 2-0 down and was punished with a red card by referee Manuel Angel Perez Hernandez, as he left the field to chants of “assassin” from Tenerife fans.

Social media has called for Owono to receive a lifetime ban from football, with reports in the local media in Tenerife claiming that The Homicide Group of the National Police in Santa Cruz is already investigating the circumstances of De Miguel's death.

While there are thankfully no precedents established in a tragic case like this in Spanish football, Article 142 of the Spanish Penal Code distinguishes between manslaughter due to gross negligence and manslaughter due to less serious negligence.

If proven, gross negligence can carry a prison sentence of up to four years for Owono, while the lesser charge may simply result in a fine.

The Spanish Football Federation’s Disciplinary Code says that players found to have committed violent conduct during play and inflicted serious injury can be banned for anywhere between four and 12 matches.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

De Miguel was knocked to the floor after his chest collided with the knee of Owono, following the Equatorial Guinea international rushing from his goal to meet the forward.

Medical help was urgently flagged by De Miguel's team-mates, with the player's condition originally described as “stable, given the seriousness of the condition” on Monday night.

Tenerife released a second statement in the early hours of Tuesday morning to state that De Miguel had “deteriorated neurologically”, before confirming later on Tuesday morning that he had passed away in hospital.

Owono was said to have been crying and praying in the dressing room after the match was abandoned, and has since deleted his Instagram account after being flooded with abuse.

Equatorial Guinean Football Federation president, Venancio Tomas Ndong Micha, has issued his “full solidarity and support” to the goalkeeper, while expressing condolences for the loss of De Miguel.

Andorra centre-back Lautaro Spatz, meanwhile, released a statement to support his team-mate, claiming “he would never ‌intentionally ⁠hurt anyone”.

#982. Football Daily | Como turn on the style and hammer nine past out-of-focus Lens

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

A consistent criticism levelled at Como is that they are simply not “Italian” enough to be a bona fide Serie A club. Bankrolled by an Indonesian ciggy manufacturer, their president has helpfully likened their multi-hubbed business model to that of the Walt Disney Company. In Cesc Fàbregas they have a Spanish coach and their starting XI against Lens in Bigger Cup on Wednesday didn’t feature a single Italian. To add insult to injury, they also thrashed their hosts 9-1 in a show of outright vulgarity that will have had Serie A traditionalists gesticulating angrily. Piling on the hurt against already-humiliated opposition has never been the Italian way, unless both teams have formally agreed to it before the game kicks off.

Still, if the Como squad was low on homegrown players, they certainly looked the part upon their arrival at Stade Bollaert-Delelis, stepping off their team coach and inspecting the pitch looking like an escape party from a Milan fashion week runway. Due in no small part to the club’s official partnership with Rome’s haute couture menswear house Brioni, Fàbregas and his globetrotting ensemble looked impossibly stylish in bespoke double-breasted suits, knitted cotton-silk-cashmere long-sleeve polos and soft slip-on nubuck loafers (sans socks, of course), thoughtfully accessorised with designer shades even though it was already practically dark.

While their pitch walk served as an ironic counterweight to domestic football debate, once Como’s players had swapped their designer duds for studs, they reverted to a brand of intense front-foot football that couldn’t have been less catenaccio, leaving their hapless French hosts chasing shadows. The 9-1 [NINE – Football Daily Vidiprinter] victory was the biggest winning margin in Bigger Cup history, with Como’s only dampener on their evening coming in the form of a thunderous volley from Lens’ Ruben Aguilar. To make up for this crushing disappointment, Como’s final two goals were scored by Mattia Liberali and Matteo Papaccioli, a pair of teenage substitutes who could only have been more Italian if they’d celebrated by wheeling away on a couple of Vespas.

Despite being the highest-spending team in Serie A for the past two seasons, Como have pulled off the impressive feat of building a brilliant squad comprised largely of players this email had never heard of until they put Manchester United to the sword a fortnight ago. In Nico Paz, they have a genuine superstar in the making, while their highest-profile summer signings were Trevoh Chalobah and Moise Kean, who were absent from the travelling party due to knack. Despite witnessing his excellent side become only the second team in Bigger Cup history to score nine goals in one game (we’ll save you a Google: Bayern Munich), Fàbregas went full Billy Buzzkill to ensure his players don’t lose the run of themselves.

“It is a wonderful night for Como, for all our fans and many lads here who are at the start of their careers, but they need to keep their feet on the ground [and in their expensive hand-stitched loafers – Football Daily Ed], be humble, keep learning and not think everything will go well from here on,” he harrumphed, before taking time out to lavish praise on one individual. “I’m angry over the goal we conceded, as we changed something in our defending with the three substitutions. Plus it was scored by a former teammate; I played with Ruben Aguilar at Monaco and I told him I’d never seen you score a goal like that before!” It was indeed the pick of the 10, even if clawing proceedings back to 7-1 felt a bit like throwing a pebble at an approaching Death Star. With nine goals, no socks and a furious head coach demanding perfection, Como’s Mickey Mouse Club is beginning to look terrifyingly real.

Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta is determined to keep the core of his title-winning team

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta has blocked two outgoings from North London this January.

That's according to new reports that claim the champions are having to fend off interest from European giants for some of their biggest stars who have started the season slowly.

With the Gunners now top of the league and in a strong position to go deep in the Champions League, it appears that Arteta wants to keep the squad that won him the Premier League last term.

It may only just be November, but Arsenal midfielder Martin Zubimendi has been linked with an Emirates Stadium exit this January since the transfer window last closed.

The 2026 World Cup winner signed for Arteta last summer ahead of the likes of Liverpool, Real Madrid and Barcelona in a huge coup for the club, but has already found himself fourth in the pecking order in midfield, following the emergence of Myles Lewis-Skelly as an option in the engine room and the signing of Bruno Guimaraes over the summer.

Now, Sport Witness have reported that Arteta has had to block Zubimendi leaving in the winter window along with Piero Hincapie, whose start to the season has been interrupted by injury and the excellent form of fellow left-back, Riccardo Calafiori.

Hincapie originally joined on loan from Bayer Leverkusen in the same window as Zubimendi, becoming a valuable first-teamer by the end of the season and starting in the Champions League final ahead of Calafiori, before the Gunners made his signing permanent.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Now, reports from Spain have claimed that Barcelona would like to bring the versatile Ecuadorian to Catalonia in the midst of their defensive crisis – but that Arteta doesn't want to deplete his squad and sanction the sale.

The Gunners boss is equally “reluctant” to let Zubimendi go, having invested a lot of effort in his signing and fought off heavy competition, with FourFourTwo understanding that Arsenal see his role potentially increasing as the season progresses.

Last term, the Basque controller was almost ever-present alongside Declan Rice in the middle of the park, before suffering burnout and dropping to the bench in favour of Lewis-Skelly – with Arteta recognising that he could well push himself into the first-team picture once again, if the reverse happens this season.

The Premier League champions understand that to compete for the biggest prizes this season, they will likely need to bring in players in January rather than sell, having left themselves somewhat short in attacking areas over the summer.

Gabriel Martinelli, Gabriel Jesus and Leandro Trossard all left before the season began, with just Christos Tzolis replacing the trio and Eberechi Eze given more of a chance to play on the left wing.

Arsenal travel to Slavia Prague as Champions League action continues tonight.

Chris Billam-Smith and Cheavon Clarke finished the ceremonial weigh-in with a wide-eyed staredown.

Billam-Smith maintained a steely, unblinking glare until Clarke looked away.

They box on Saturday night at the Copper Box Arena, live on Sky Sports, and Billam-Smith pledged simply that the fight would be "a violent one".

Does that mean he intends to end it inside the distance? "Absolutely."

Clarke though has beaten Billam-Smith before, defeating him twice in amateur bouts a decade ago.

"Twenty-five-year-old me will be very happy tomorrow night," Billam-Smith said.

He might have beaten the Bournemouth man as an amateur, but Clarke has been overshadowed by Billam-Smith as a pro. He wants to change that on Saturday.

"After tomorrow night you guys will be talking my name," Clarke said. "It's going to be explosive.

Shane Mosley Jr missed weight on the first attempt for his middleweight clash with Denzel Bentley.

Mosley fights Bentley in the chief support to Billam-Smith vs Clarke on Saturday.

The son of boxing legend Shane Mosley, the American contender took to the scales on Friday morning for the official weigh-in.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Tall and big for the weight, Mosley looked gaunt as he stepped on to the scales. Stripping to shave off some additional weight, he stepped on to the scales behind a screen but was still one pound over the middleweight limit for his first attempt.

London's Bentley looked in fine condition as he hit the 160lb limit exactly. He stayed to watch Mosley return to the scales. The American took almost the full hour to shed the final pound but did so, having to strip again. The fight is on.

"He's made the weight now, hopefully rehydrates nice and healthy and we have a good fight tomorrow," Bentley told Sky Sports. "It's not his first time making middleweight. I feel fit and well that gives me confidence, the fact that I feel so good.

"That's what makes it a good fight, both of us are confident. We haven't got to be at each other's throats to make a fight. We're both respectful but we're letting each other know I think I'm coming out the victor."

Mosley Jr dismissed the weight miss as a 'miscalculation'.

"I just miscalculated a little bit but we got it done," he said later. "I win this fight on points, outclass him.

Clarke made weight easily, scaling 198.8lbs. For Billam-Smith it was a harder cut but he came in at 199.5lbs.

Both Billam-Smith and Clarke are coming off thrilling wins, beating Ryan Rozicki and Jack Massey respectively in barnstorming bouts in Bournemouth in June. That put the two on a collision course.

Zuffa Boxing promoter Dana White told Sky Sports: "It's always about putting on the best fights with the best fighters. After his showing in the main event in Bournemouth was incredible. "Styles make fights and stylistically that should be a fun fight. CBS and Rozicki was one of the craziest fights I've ever seen and it really put those two on the map now in the boxing scene. So hopefully we get another one of those."

During a visit to Singapore, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Europe and Germany want to increase free trade with open competition, reliability and a rules-based order.

This blog is now closed. Below is a roundup of the top stories in Germany on Tuesday, October 27, 2026:

On the first day of his farewell tour in China, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier urged the German business community to act with confidence in the Chinese market.

"When you travel in China, you're amazed at how highly Germany and German technology are still valued here," he said in Hefei. "That's why we can act with confidence in these markets."

Steinmeier did not bring any companies with him to China as part of his delegation, as his final trip was intended to focus on culture and science.

Nevertheless, the first day of the trip in Hefei, the capital of Anhui Province, revolved primarily around the economy. Steinmeier visited the Volkswagen China Technology Company (VCTC). About three years ago, Europe's largest automaker opened a research center for electric mobility there, which today employs 3,000 people.

Johannes Volkmann, a lawmaker accompanying Steinmeier in China, warned that the German economy must not "lose its leadership in innovation."

"I'm taking this call to action with me from here to do more to improve competitive conditions at home," he said, adding that Germany must avoid creating new dependencies "by allowing innovation and value creation to take place only outside Europe."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Steinmeier called for Europe to reposition itself and reorganize its economic instruments with its growing trade deficit with China in mind.

"The trade surplus that China is accumulating naturally causes us concern because the successful model of economic cooperation is becoming unbalanced," he said. "We must strive to ensure that economic cooperation does not come to an end, but that it continues — to the mutual benefit of both sides."

Germany's trade deficit with China amounted to just under €90 billion ($100 billion) in 2025. According to the Federal Statistical Office, China exported goods worth €170.6 billion to Germany, and German exports to China amounted to €81.3 billion.

Across the 27-member EU, the deficit amounted to almost €197 billion in the first half of 2026, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic.

Additional reporting by Rosalia Romaniec in Hefei.

A German court denied a defense request to end the trial of a former Ukrainian army officer who stands accused of sabotaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines.

Serhii Kuznietsov, 50, went on trial this month at the Hamburg state court, charged with causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public services and being an "accomplice to war crimes" by attacking civilian infrastructure.

Prosecutors accuse him of being the ringleader of the destruction, considered one of Europe's biggest acts of post-World War II sabotage. He is alleged to have carried out the explosions together with six others.

His lawyers said the charges should be dismissed, arguing that, as a former soldier, Kuznietsov was obligated by Ukrainian law not to speak for national security reasons and could face severe penalties in Ukraine if he did. They argued that, under German law, anyone who cannot speak on his or her own behalf cannot be convicted.

The Hamburg court ruled Kuznietsov's defense was not limited under German law and that freedom to testify is not limited by a foreign country's conditions of service.

The undersea explosions on September 26, 2022, damaged the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, which brought Russian natural gas to Germany until Moscow cut off supplies in August 2022.

The blasts also damaged the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never went into service. Germany suspended the pipeline's certification process shortly before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Italian authorities detained Kuznietsov last year. He was publicly named in extradition proceedings that led to his transfer to Germany in November.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has denied allegations that his country was involved in the pipeline blasts.

German carmaker Mercedes-Benz has cut its forecast for 2026, with difficult market conditions in China and higher fourth-quarter cost expectations set to negatively impact profits, the company said on Tuesday.

Markets were quick to take note of the announcement, and Mercedes shares dropped 3.4% in trading on Tuesday morning.

The move makes Mercedes the third big German carmaker to lower its outlook for 2026 after BMW and VW took similar steps.

Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Kaellenius has called on German employees to work more without pay while also expanding manufacturing operations in Hungary, where he said costs are about 70% lower than in Germany.

Mercedes currently expects an adjusted car profit margin of 2% to 3% in 2026, compared to the 3% to 5% in the previous guidance.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Like many German automakers, Mercedes has faced weak sales in China. German carmakers have struggled in the world's largest car market with sluggish demand and increased competition from local manufacturers.

Mercedes vehicle deliveries in China — last year already at their lowest level since 2016 — fell a further 29% in the nine months to the end of September.

Mercedes also released third-quarter figures earlier than planned, which showed that the company generated just €172 million ($191 million) in free cash flow from its vehicle business, down on the €422 million forecast by financial market experts.

Before interest and tax, Mercedes posted an operating profit of €1.77 billion — more than double the €750 million recorded a year earlier, according to the preliminary figures. But last year's stats were significantly impacted by one-time expenses, especially related to job cuts and legal disputes.

Adjusted for one-off items, the operating profit margin in the passenger car business stood at 2.5%, down on the 4.8% recorded a year earlier.

The German agency responsible for finding a final repository for nuclear waste (BGE) has eliminated five states from its search.

Berlin, Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saxony and Saarland were deemed unsuitable for long-term radioactive waste storage.

In a report issued Tuesday, the BGE said it had limited its search to 5% of Germany, down from 25% in 2025. The federal agency aims to suggest suitable locations for final evaluation by the end of 2027.

Regions in northern, northwestern, southern and eastern Germany remain under consideration as locations for final storage facilities.

Germany's nuclear waste is currently stored in 16 above-ground interim storage facilities.

The BGE assessments evaluate regions' geological conditions and their ability to safely contain highly radioactive material. Granite, salt, and clay are generally considered potentially suitable types of rock and areas with damaged or compromised subsurface conditions, places with mines or volcanos have been active, are not eligible as final disposal sites.

Germany needs to find a repository for approximately 27,000 cubic meters of highly radioactive nuclear waste generated over more than 60 years of nuclear power generation. The site is expected to ensure safety for 1 million years. The last German nuclear power plants were decommissioned in April 2023.

BGE said its goal remains finding the site that offers the highest level of safety for highly radioactive waste.

The agency's recommendations, however, are not legally binding and it will be up to German lawmakers to determine the final disposal site.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Convicted right-wing terrorist Beate Zschäpe's request for early release from prison was denied with a court ruling that she would remain behind bars for at least nine more years.

Munich's Higher Regional Court on Tuesday set her minimum term at at least 24 years and refused to suspend the sentence to probation. By determining her guilt to be particularly severe, the court effectively ruled out her release after 15 years, which, including her time in pretrial detention, would have expired this year.

The Munich court said Zschäpe, currently 51, still had a good chance of leaving prison alive.

The decision is not yet legally binding, and the defense and the Federal Prosecutor's Office can appeal.

Zschäpe had been sentenced to life in prison in 2018 as an accomplice in the National Socialist Underground (NSU) murders that killed 10 people, mainly individuals with an immigrant background as well as a police officer.

The terror group went undetected for a decade. Zschäpe's fellow NSU members, Uwe Mundlos and Uwe Böhnhardt, injured several people with bomb attacks in Cologne and killed themselves to avoid arrest in 2011.

Under normal conditions, a convict who receives a life sentence in Germany can apply for parole after 15 years.

Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has won football's most prestigious individual prize, beating Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite an uneven league.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, along with his counterparts from France, Italy, Poland and the UK, authored an op-ed calling Russia "the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability."

In the article, published online and in Tuesday's Tagesspiegel newspaper, the defense ministers wrote they "share a deep conviction" that European countries need to do more to ensure their own security and aim to build "a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO."

The ministers, however, added that the United States would remain an "indispensable ally."

The pronouncement comes as many in Europe are wary of US President Donald Trump's commitment to the NATO military alliance.

The US leader has threatened to leave the group and to seize control of Greenland, a territory of fellow NATO member Denmark. US presidents have repeatedly called for European NATO members to contribute more to the alliance's military capabilities.

As US support for Ukraine also appears to waver, the five defense ministers reiterated their political, military and financial support for Kyiv as it fights of Russia's full-scale invasion.

In Singapore, to start a four-day business-oriented trip that will also bring him to Japan and South Korea, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said it was up to European and Asian nations to find their spot amid a changing global order.

"We must assert our interests in an international environment shaped by renewed great-power rivalry," Merz said.

With a view to unpredictable tariffs imposed by the United States under President Donald Trump and trade restrictions from China, Merz emphasized the stability offered by Germany and the rest of Europe.

"This is a deliberate counterpoint to what we are currently seeing. We want to do things differently, and we want to show that there is a better way," Merz said, adding that Europe sought to expand partnerships to increase free trade with open competition, reliability and a rules-based order.

He also called for increased international investment and cooperation.

"Under the federal government I lead, investment opportunities will be continuously improved," Merz said following a meeting with Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong. "I encounter a great deal of confidence here in Germany and in Europe as locations for investment."

The German leader called for a new free-trade agreement between the 27-member European Union and the Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), comprising 12 countries across five continents, including Australia, Canada, Japan, Mexico and the United Kingdom. Neither the United States nor China is part of the CPTPP.

For his part, Wong said investment in Germany and Europe would continue.

"Many of our investors, including our sovereign wealth funds, have been investing in Germany for a long time," Wong said. "They will continue to invest because they are confident that, in the long term, Germany and Europe have potential."

Merz and Wong agreed their nations would work to expand cooperation in security and defense as well as trade, investment, sustainable energy and artificial intelligence.

#977. Shola Ameobi: ‘I thought: how can I be most useful to Newcastle? Then the cog started turning’

From experiencing racism growing up in Newcastle to becoming a derby hero and now a member of the executive team, the former striker has been on a remarkable journey

“There were times where I feared for my life as a kid, being harassed and chased by different groups of people,” Shola Ameobi says. “There were situations where I had to sprint to get away from groups of lads who didn’t like me because of what I looked like.”

Ameobi is recalling growing up in Newcastle during the late 1980s and 1990s, having moved from Nigeria aged six. There were lots of moments like that.

“It was almost as if I had to hide myself to be able to do what I love to do,” he says. “It wasn’t a very nice feeling, having to worry about getting from A to B. It was just part of my world. I had to be more aware of my surroundings and what I was doing.”

Ameobi’s “A” was often the family home, situated within a few pitch lengths of Newcastle’s St James’ Park, and “B” was frequently the club’s base at the time in Benwell, where he would head for academy training.

“It built incredible resilience in me,” he says. “That really helped me in a sporting context in my career, but also as a person, understanding that, irrespective of what people thought of me, what really mattered was the value I put on myself.”

That young boy running in fear became the scorer of 79 goals in 397 appearances for Newcastle including seven against their local rivals, Sunderland. The likelihood is that some of those he fled from while wearing a club tracksuit subsequently cheered him.

Since July, Ameobi has been Newcastle’s head of corporate affairs, after seven years as the loans coordinator. His role is to ensure “we’re doing things that are valuable not only to us as a football club but to the region”.

He adds: “We want to make this club the heartbeat of this city. But by being the heartbeat of the city, it’s making sure we integrate well into everything the city is about, whether that’s civically, whether that’s through our sport or through our community engagement.”

Ameobi’s job switch followed the 100-day review conducted by the CEO, David Hopkinson. At the end of a preliminary discussion, Hopkinson told Ameobi to take the weekend to consider things. But Ameobi, while grateful for the “level of trust and commitment”, pushed back, wanting to consider what the role would look like in practice. Six months and plentiful discussions later, he accepted.

For Ameobi, the leap to an executive position was not as huge as it might appear. He started his previous role in the Mike Ashley days and built that department “from nothing”, he says. “That’s really helped me understand how to business-plan and build a team.”

Ameobi has been part of the Premier League’s Black participants advisory group since it formed in 2019. Its successes include implementing the No Room for Racism action plan in 2021 – this weekend marks the second of two match rounds this month dedicated to the initiative – and the pilot launch of the player to executive pathways scheme in 2022. That is designed to help those from underrepresented groups into executive roles and Ameobi was part of the initial seven-strong cohort.

“It gave me a really good framework,” he says. “It took us through, at a very high level, what the different streams of executive work look like, whether that’s finance, brand, the future of working, how organisations work. That gave me a little bit of confidence, if I’m honest, more than anything, to go: ‘Actually, a lot of the things I’m already doing translate into that world.’

“One of the biggest things was working in a pressurised environment, which is what I’ve done for 20 years, and learning how that can really help you in those moments when things get a little squirrelly, when they aren’t going as planned.”

Completing the programme fuelled a fire in Ameobi that had flickered for two decades. In November 2006, having struggled with a hip injury for several years, he had career-saving surgery. The resulting time out was “the start of my thought process beyond the football pitch”. Whether he would return to playing at his previous level, or at all, was uncertain. So, Ameobi’s thoughts turned to: “How can I best be useful to my teammates and this football club? That’s when the cog started turning.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“Football wasn’t always going to be there so who am I outside of the footballer? There were some really hard questions I had to answer during a very, very difficult time. There were some dark moments.”

Ameobi navigated those moments with the help of a psychologist and by leaning on his family. “I’ve always been fascinated with leadership, right from an early age,” he says. “My father was a leader of a church and he’s been the biggest influence of my life when it comes to leadership and how to lead well.”

He cites the late Sir Bobby Robson, who gave him his professional debut aged 18, and Alan Pardew, who managed him at Newcastle and Crystal Palace, as footballing influences. The former “still to this day has such an impact on the way I think about the game, the way I think about the person more than what you’re doing”, while the latter “used me to channel my leadership within the dressing room and wider squad to help him deal with some of the issues we were going through”.

Ameobi holds a master’s in strategic leadership and it is obvious at an event to celebrate the supporters’ group The Black Geordie Club that he is a natural with people. There is a presence to him, a warmth, that puts others at ease.

He is unrelenting in wanting to use his position to improve society. He grew up watching Andy Cole at Newcastle and memories of Tino Asprilla’s 1997 Champions League hat-trick against Barcelona bring the broadest of smiles. “That was the moment where time stood still. It was almost like I said to myself: ‘What’s wrong with you, Shola? You should be giving everything to be there.’

“You need to feel like you belong, you need to see yourself there, and that is so important when it comes to inspiration and people who aspire to be great in whatever sphere.

“It’s so important those who are in those positions give back and share their experience and share what helped them get to where they’re at. Being a young Black kid who has walked the walk throughout the club, from youth team to first team and now into this executive role, I want to show anything’s possible for anybody.

“Part of the reason I want to continue to push myself is because, yes, I want to be successful, but I want to show that anything’s possible if you’ve got the hunger, irrespective of what you look like and where you come from. I want to be an inspiration to the next generation.”

Manchester City’s start to the 2026/27 season under Enzo Maresca has received a blow, with reports emerging that Rayan Ait-Nouri’s representatives are actively and publicly seeking a way out of the Etihad Stadium for their client.

The Algerian international, widely regarded as one of Europe’s more dynamic attacking full-backs, has found himself out of the side under the Italian. Frustration has seemingly now reached a point of no return.

According to L'Equipe, which was subsequently relayed by Get French Football News, Ait-Nouri’s camp has lost patience with Maresca’s handling of the 25-year-old.

The player's entourage delivered a blunt assessment of his current predicament, declaring: "He can’t remain in a situation where his talent is wasted."

That admission provides a window into the growing disconnect between Maresca and certain members his squad. Since taking the reins at the Etihad, the former Chelsea boss has adhered to a tactical style that has bypassed Ait-Nouri’s natural overlapping instincts.

Ait-Nouri’s sidelining could be framed as particularly confusing given Man City’s recent struggles to break down low-block defences - a scenario where the Algerian’s ball-carrying ability and final-third delivery usually prove effective.

Instead, he has been restricted to cameo appearances and domestic cup starts, a downgrade in status that has not gone unnoticed by those representing him.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Crossing isn’t exactly a dying art, but it has certainly become rarer to see the more ambitious, attack-minded teams swing crosses into the box from open play.

It just isn’t de rigueur to try something so low-percentage, something so unfashionably anti-aesthetic.

But two of the most attacking clubs (with two of the most modern, zeitgeisty tacticians) pivoted to crossing at the weekend, so it is worth considering whether this is the beginning of a new trend that will catch on.

Fashion, after all, plays an outsized role in tactical theory in the Premier League, and if Brighton and Liverpool are doing it, then it must be Smart and Good.

Liverpool’s 12 open-play crosses in the first half on Sunday were the most any team have managed against Arsenal since November 2020. By the 42nd minute, when Alex Mac Allister should have scored with a header from what was their 19th cross (open or set-piece) of the match, Liverpool had almost quadrupled the five crosses they made in the whole game against Brighton the weekend before.

Brighton weren’t as consistent in their 2-0 victory over Manchester City, but there was a clear tactical plan to switch the play with long diagonals into the (very wide) wingers as often as possible. Fabian Hurzeler appeared to see City’s not-actually-full-backs as the weak spot, and it worked, leading directly to the winning goal.

Liverpool and Brighton had different reasons for their strategies, although the end result was the same: both knew that by getting balls into the box they could sew chaos. Brighton’s winner came via a deflected half-clearance, while Arsenal’s defence regularly made first contact but, now on the back foot, were penned in by the loose second ball (at their most dishevelled, Jurrien Timber pulled on Alexander Isak’s shirt).

As Iraola put it: “We’ve put them under pressure, we’ve put them inside the box, we’ve put them there.”

Arsenal, uncomfortable, were pushed back into the box; were 'put there'. It is a simple, albeit unfashionable, idea that others may choose to follow.

#973. Ian Holloway’s circus: why the manager’s antics are no laughing matter for fans

Swindon manager has a history of viral outbursts but fans want a united club and manager they can support

In Ian Holloway’s often madcap managerial orbit, this was simply the latest in a steady succession of eccentric outbursts. Eyes bulging as he spoke, he boomed the letter “D” and promptly stabbed himself in the chest with an imaginary dagger. Next came the letter “M” alongside a blow from another invisible knife. Finally, a “W” followed by a jab to the heart. “Dead. Man. Walking,” he declared, pausing for effect between words and briefly falling into an Oscar-worthy zombie stupor. “That’s how it feels.”

To an offbeat press conference genre containing seagulls following trawlers and self-proclaimed special ones, it was a crazy new entry worthy of its subsequent viral nature. Holloway at his finest.

The clip was widely shared, there is every chance you saw it this month. The general perception, from those of a neutral stance, was that one of football’s great characters had lost the plot. To those in the room, there was a sense that it was merely the exuberant mannerisms of a quirky manager during a tricky period. But for a large section of Swindon fans, it prompted an unamused eye roll. Here we go again. The circus tent is pitched firmly in town.

Supporting a Holloway-led club is an interesting assignment. Within weeks of taking the Swindon job two years ago on Sunday, he began constructing a hostile wall towards fans by reminding them that they could “go bowling” if they did not like his methods. Last December, he had to be restrained by his players during an altercation with a fan, while he has made a habit of telling them to “jog on” if overly vocal in their criticism.

When his side picked up a much-needed point against Walsall last week, the goalkeeping coach held him back from another confrontation with supporters. Asked about it, he goaded reporters into putting his address online so that disgruntled fans could have it out with him: “I don’t really care anymore.” So, when season‑ticket holders found their phones pinging with amused messages containing the same viral Holloway zombie clip, their lack of laughter could be forgiven.

“When you get these soundbites from Ian Holloway, outside the Swindon Town world it’s all about what a great character he is, how he says it like it is, and how it must be great to have him as manager,” says Rich Pullen, founder and co-host of the largest Swindon podcast, Loathed Strangers. “But, to a growing percentage of the Swindon community, it’s exhausting and it takes away from any of the good.

“If Swindon win, post-match he often uses it as an opportunity to have a go at the fans. It’s got to the stage where you can’t even enjoy a win without Ian Holloway being unable to hold himself from criticising fans. The easy thing to do is ignore him, but it’s almost impossible because he is everywhere. He goes viral and everyone always thinks: ‘Oh, isn’t that funny.’ Well, no. People are tired of the excess noise.”

This time last week, there was a thought that the M4 derby homecoming trip to Bristol Rovers on Saturday might hasten a possible end to Holloway’s Swindon tenure. Winless in eight games in all competitions, the discontent was not expected to abate on the preceding midweek trip to high-flying Barnet. The 3-1 victory that followed – Barnet’s first league defeat of the season – was a huge shock, thanks in no small part to the heroics of the goalkeeper, Connor Ripley, who recently declared the whole squad would “run through a brick wall” for Holloway.

Swindon might have followed it with another win, at Rovers’ Memorial Stadium, only for Matty Virtue to miss an open goal 90 seconds into the match. The forgettable goalless draw that played out at least extended Swindon’s unbeaten run to three games and kept them safely mid-table in League Two. Holloway was right to savour the improved performances, but the malaise runs deeper.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The manager had said something far more significant immediately after his viral soundbite when he continued: “The owner’s a dead man walking as well and that over‑complicates everything here.”

Even those seeking a more composed figure in Holloway’s place agree the manager is just one cog in a machine many argue has been misfiring for some time. Days after the zombie rant, the Swindon Town Supporters Trust declared the club had “lost our soul, our hope, our passion”, and urged Holloway’s comments about the Australian owner, Clem Morfuni, to “be a wake-up call”.

Since saving the club from probable administration in 2021, Morfuni has become a target of increasing fan indignation, failing to sell up and adding millions to the club’s debt. “Whilst the short-term focus may be on Ian Holloway, the bigger picture is above the role of the manager,” concluded the Trust, pointing to “a wedge with supporters so obvious that even the manager openly talks about it”.

In such a context, the uptick in form is merely one – albeit very welcome – aspect among wider misgivings. Because what fans really want is a united club and manager they can get behind; not to go jogging on.

#972. Harry Kane: Ballon d’Or for Bayern Munich striker

Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has won football's most prestigious individual prize, beating Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite an uneven league.

To most Bayern Munich fans under the age of 40, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge was the club CEO who regularly spoke his mind. Fans with longer memories, or a better grasp of Bavarian football history, recall Rummenigge as one of the club's all-time great players. He was also the last Bayern man to win the Ballon d'Or — in 1981. The last Bundesliga player to win was Borussia Dortmund's Matthias Sammer, in 1996.

That long drought ended on Monday, with Harry Kane, born 12 years after Rummenigge's win, picking up the 2026 trophy at a ceremony held, as a one-off, in his native London.

"I am almost speechless. Being here in London has made it extra special,” he said on stage.

Not many people would have thought it, and maybe even I wouldn't have thought I'd be this far," Kane later told British sports streaming plaftorm DAZN.

Lamine Yamal, the prodigious Barcelona and Spain forward who won the Euros at 16, finished third. At the end of the 2025-26 season, on which the award is judged, Yamal won the World Cup with Spain as well as the La Liga title. Kylian Mbappe came in second.

Kane's 73 goals for club and country last season made for a strong case, and the Bundesliga's most expensive signing of all time has already racked up 156 goals in 159 games for the serial German champions. But it's not just the numbers that tell the story, according to his club coach.

"People in England saw him as a goalscorer during his time playing there," Vincent Kompany said of Kane last season. "We've seen other qualities too, such as his footballing intelligence. We can appreciate that now — it was perhaps somewhat underestimated in England. He's like a fine wine that improves with age. I also enjoy that aspect of his game."

Kane continues to improve at 33, a point when many footballers start to regress. Though he is helped by being more reliant on guile and technique than pace, Kane's professionalism is key to staying at the top, according to his Bayern teammate Serge Gnabry.

"He always has the right attitude, always leads the way and sets the tone," Gnabry said ahead of Bayern's 2-2 draw in the Champions League against Arsenal last week. "He never strays from his path, helps the team with his performance and is a top-tier player."

Kane scored a penalty in that match and provided a sensational pass from which Alphonso Davies scored Bayern's opener, another reminder of his all-round game. "The pass was one of my best ones," Kane said after the match. "I knew Phonzy [Davies] would be able to get there with his speed. Whatever I can do to help the team, I'll do. At the moment, it seems to be with assists more than goals."

That attitude has been with Kane from the start. His first-ever coach, Dave Bricknell, from Ridgeway Rovers, an amateur club in northeast London, told DW after Kane joined Bayern from Spurs in 2023: "Harry's mentality is his greatest strength. He doesn't let anything worry him. If he misses a chance, he doesn't care — he will go and score from another chance."

His England coach, Thomas Tuchel, has also emphasized Kane's leadership. "He is the first one to push everyone, and that is his mindset, and he became a very, very hardworking forward on top of his finishing skills, Tuchel said in September as Kane extended his England goal-scoring record against the Czech Republic. "He is a complete package."

There are detractors who point to perceived "stat-padding," or scoring against inferior opponents in international qualifiers and in the Bundesliga, where there are fewer elite teams and a lot less money, than in England. Though Kane's ratio of 213 goals in 320 games in the Premier League is a little off his Bundesliga stats, it bears comparison with any other player in the history of the league.

Kane winning the award is also a boost in profile for the Bundesliga, which has been unable to keep pace, both commercially and on the pitch, with other top European leagues of late, particularly the Premier League and La Liga.

Winning it in a league outside of England or Spain perhaps makes Kane's feat even greater. Other than Ousmane Dembele, who won it last year after Paris Saint-Germain's Champions League win, and Lionel Messi, a serial Ballon d'Or winner, the last player to take the Ballon d'Or for a season played outside England or Spain was was Kaka at AC Milan in 2007, when Italy's Serie A was considered a stronger league.

Kane's career hasn't been straightforward, something he admitted in his speech. After signing his first senior contract with Spurs in July 2010, he was sent out on various loans to lower league sides between 2011-2013 without ever making a huge impression.

"My journey wasn't straightforward. I wasn't the kid who went straight to the top. I had to experience the downs, I had a lot of loan moves, I had to fight my way to be the very best right now, and I hope that can give you determination as well," Kane said in his speech.

For former teammate Jermain Defoe, who also coached Kane at Spurs, those experiences were formative.

"You have to show a resilience. It's not easy when you go out on loan, it can feel like you're being rejected by the club that you are at, which isn't the case," he told DW in 2023, before adding that Kane's ability was always clear.

"When he joined up with the [Tottenham] first team, you could see the potential," Defoe said. "He was always a good finisher, always hit the ball clean. … With Harry you already knew, he had that natural instinct and always felt comfortable in front of goal."

Those goals have, after a failure to win a trophy in England, led to two Bundesliga titles and a German Cup. But success with England remains elusive after a 2026 World Cup exit in the semifinals. Kane will be 35 by the time of the next Euros, in the UK and Ireland in 2028, and has a deal with Bayern until the following year. His form since joining Bayern suggests that he could get better still.

This article was first published on October 22, 2026. It was updated on October 27 after Harry Kane won the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

The Reds lost their way after the teenager’s withdrawal in Sunday’s defeat to Arsenal as the midfielder shone on his first ever Premier League start

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola grabbed Trey Nyoni and threw him in at the deep end. Sink or swim was the aim of the game. And the teenager kept his head above water, and then some.

The teenager made his first ever Premier League start on Sunday afternoon. The call was well deserved following a fine showing against Chelsea in the EFL Cup.

That it came against defending champions Arsenal was a huge show of faith in the midfielder. The Reds may have fallen to a narrow 1-0 home defeat to the Gunners, but Nyoni’s 59-minute display proved he’s ready for regular minutes in this Liverpool side.

You’d be forgiven for overlooking Nyoni’s showing at Anfield. Declan Rice, after all, was the star performer on Merseyside. Mikel Arteta’s ‘Master-of-all-Trades’ midfield man put in a dominant display in the middle of the park.

The assist for Kai Havertz’s one and only goal was the cherry on the icing atop the Arsenal cake.

Yet despite coming up against, arguably, one of the best midfielders in world football, Nyoni wasn’t overawed. Rather, he rose to the occasion to deliver a performance that perhaps convinced Iraola he is worthy of a starting spot at the expense of either Alexis Mac Allister or Ryan Gravenberch.

“I just tried to go out there and do what I do, tried to get on the ball as much as possible and bring the team forwards,” Nyoni told the official Liverpool website about making his debut in such a blockbuster event. Many would have been overwhelmed by the spotlight that came from such a moment. Nyoni, though, was buoyed on by the welcome of Arsenal.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The 19-year-old ended the game with the best pass success rate (96.4%) of all starters in Sunday’s match. Only teammates Virgil van Dijk (67) and Mac Allister (61) made more passes than the academy product (56). The former pair played the full 90, whereas the latter was withdrawn on the hour mark.

Nyoni was dictating the tempo in the middle of the park, and driving Liverpool forward. Only Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya (46) made more forward passes than the youngster (24) at the weekend. Fourteen line-breaking passes was the most during his time on the pitch.

Iraola’s decision to withdraw Nyoni in place of the returning Dominik Szoboszlai meant that, for a 15-minute spell, Liverpool ceded momentum as they struggled to gain a foothold on the game.

From the 76th-minute onwards, they again dominated possession, even if it amounted to nothing, but Nyoni’s substitution saw the tie swing back in Arsenal’s favour at a crucial time in the clash. It’s within this 15-minute window where Arteta’s men begin to turn the screw in games. Only Manchester United (33) have had more shots than Arsenal (26) between minutes 60 and 75. Twenty-four chances created ranks top.

Liverpool needed a player who was comfortable in possession to ensure Arsenal were unable to build upon Havertz’s early strike. Of course, the momentum swing didn’t amount to another Gunners goal. Conversely, Liverpool would have enjoyed a more comfortable period of play had Nyoni remained on the pitch.

He brings some much-needed composure in a key area, a quality that had been found wanting following the departure of Curtis Jones. The sidelined Ryan Gravenberch brings the drive from deep, while Mac Allister offers the nitty-gritty, off the ball work to help protect the defence. Nyoni, meanwhile, delivers the forward thrust with his vision and distribution, qualities that far exceed both Gravenberch and Mac Allister, particularly in a 4-2-3-1 setup.

And having been dispossessed just four times in all competitions this season, Nyoni’s press resistance is another important trait. He’s comfortable receiving the ball from the centre-backs, before turning and setting his side on the frontfoot. Even under pressure, you’d back the up-and-coming Reds star to wriggle his way out of danger.

At his age, Nyoni, physically, still has some growing to do. Iraola can be expected to manage his minutes accordingly in order to avoid injury stunting his growth. Regardless, it’s clear that Nyoni is ready for a more prominent role in this Liverpool side.

Former boss Arne Slot used Nyoni sparingly, despite speaking highly of the player. In a difficult second, and final, season in the Anfield dugout, the Dutchman opted for experience. Injuries have perhaps forced Iraola’s hand this time around, but Nyoni has grabbed the opportunity to consolidate a starting spot with both hands.
