#884. Lampard: VAR didn't do its job

Three VAR reviews went against Coventry in their defeat to Everton; James Tarkowski's hair pull on Caleb Yirenkyi was not penalised; Vitalii Mykolenko's clip on Taiwo Awoniyi also not given as a penalty; there were handball calls for Thierno Barry's second goal

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Coventry boss Frank Lampard says VAR 'didn't do its job' in his side's defeat to Everton as three reviews controversially went against his side.

Two penalty appeals and a possible handball for Everton's second goal were all reviewed by VAR officials Timothy Wood and Gary Beswick, but nothing was given. They were also not awarded on-field by referee Stuart Attwell.

Coventry opened the scoring after the two penalty appeals, but were ultimately beaten 3-1 on Merseyside on Friday Night Football.

Lampard told Sky Sports: "I hate to sound like a moaner. It's a football match and if you win the game, that can happen here. I've worked here and know the momentum swings in the game.

"I'm not trying to talk about the circumstances of the actual football, but when big decisions change games, they absolutely do. It's disappointing. VAR is there for that and it didn't do its job."

Here, we breaks down each incident and what the pundits, managers and players had to say...

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Towards the end of the first half, James Tarkowski rose to defend a high ball into the box. As he did, he caught Ethan Pinnock with an elbow, before also appearing to pull the hair of Caleb Yirenkyi.

VAR did look at the incident, especially the elbow, but nothing was given in terms of a card or a penalty.

There was no communication from the Premier League Match Centre on if the hair pull was reviewed, but there was new guidance from the Premier League this summer, which says: "A red card will be issued when there is a clear and deliberate action to pull an opponent's hair with excessive force and/or brutality.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"A yellow card will be issued if the action is deemed to be without excessive force and/or brutality.

"Referees will enhance recognition of clear holding actions that have a clear material impact, and/or non-footballing holding actions with no place on the football pitch. This includes penalising defenders where they are clearly only focused on opponents and making a holding action that is impactful on the attacker's ability to play or challenge for the ball."

"The first-half decision on Tarkowski got checked. Seeing it back, he pulls on Caleb's hair while competing with Ethan.

"I thought the rules were clear. I know they've changed the rules so it's no red card, I get that too. But he's pulling on his hair and [Yirenkyi] can't get his momentum to jump. I think it's a foul and a penalty and they decided no."

Sky Sports' Jamie Redknapp on Friday Night Football: "Yirenkyi goes up, Tarkowski gets hold of his hair. He yanks it down. Is it excessive force? Probably not, but he pulls his hair, stopping any elevation. It's a definite penalty for me.

"Yirenkyi knows he has his hair pulled. It's unusual for Tarkowski to do. It's not the best piece of defending that's for sure... It's a foul. It's not a red card anymore but it's definitely a foul."

Lee Hendrie on Sky Sports co-commentary: "There's a clear pull... Tarkowski is in the heart of this. There's an elbow, which isn't a problem, but the hair pull will raise awareness.

"You can clearly see he's utilising the hair. It's a tight one. VAR have completely not looked at it or felt the need to look at it."

Everton boss David Moyes to Sky Sports on whether he is bothered by Coventry's calls: “I’m bothered because we want it [the result] to be right, but we’ve had a few decisions recently where we don’t think have gone our way. "There was one possibly at Newcastle but there was one at Man City last season in a league game which was hugely important for us regarding getting into Europe. "Sometimes they go for you, sometimes they don’t. If they were going against me, I’d be complaining a bit more.”

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

At the start of the second half, Taiwo Awoniyi drove into the box with Vitalii Mykolenko behind him. There was some contact from behind which sent the striker down.

Referee Stuart Attwell said no penalty, while the VAR review deemed the contact to be outside the box.

"I thought the one on Taiwo running through - it's a clear foul that the referee doesn't give in-game. I can't believe that because it's clear. Maybe he waited for VAR because it was on the borderline.

"But as I see it, Taiwo's foot is entering the box and his knee and the back of his knee is on the line of the box, which is a penalty."

"It's a definite penalty and it's rubbish from the VAR. It's a poor decision. It's a definite foul, they rush it too quickly, and his foot's on the line.

"VAR said it was outside the box - but it's on the line. If you're in the line, you're in the box.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"Awoniyi puts his right foot across and then Mykolenko just gets him. It's on the line. It's a definite foul and goes over. Mykolenko goes over as well.

"Just take a breather, tell the referee to have a look at it and he will have come to a different conclusion."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

There was a question of handball before Barry's second goal which gave Everton the lead. He bundled home from Tyrique George's cross, with the ball bouncing wildly.

VAR did check the goal, but there was no conclusive evidence of handball and the goal was allowed to stand.

Friday Night Football later revealed what VAR had said about the incident. VAR official Wood said in his deliberations: "Okay, that's his side, that's definitely not hand. Confirming on-field decision of goal."

However, on Sky Sports co-commentary, Hendrie maintained he believed it was a handball and should have been ruled out.

It was a sentiment that, unsurprisingly Lampard agreed with, telling Sky Sports: "Barry's second goal comes off his hand... His last touch flicks it in the net. It was a really quick check as well. People may disagree, but it's my opinion."

When asked about it, goalscorer Barry said: "A goal is goal! I scored two goals today... It's the job of the striker to score. I'm in a good moment and I try to keep this feeling."

"We've looked at it forensically and I do think it touches his hand. But when you're asking VAR to intervene and disallow the goal, it's difficult.

"I watched it for maybe five to 10 minutes and I've come to the conclusion that I think it was, but I understand why VAR didn't give it because it's not clear and obvious enough.

"To me, it looks like it brushes his left hand, but we've been able to blow it up and look at it. A good game is a quick game and we don't want VAR to intervene and take 10 minutes.

"It's not as conclusive as we'd like to see for them [VAR] to intervene... "It brushes his fingers. It's accidental as well, does it mean to hit his hands?

"It does divert it a little bit, but if we're going to get to that point where we're forensically looking at every single thing, it becomes hard."

#883. Volkswagen logs Q3 operating loss of €5.86 billion on Porsche writedown

The Volkswagen Group has filed its worst quarterly performance since the height of the "Dieselgate" scandal in 2015. Share prices climbed in response, however, perhaps because the bad news was so well signposted.

The Volkswagen Group on Thursday posted its worst quarterly numbers in more than a decade.

The company reported an operating loss of €5.86 billion (roughly $6.53 billion) during July, August and September. One-off costs, not least a massive writedown in its stake in struggling sister company Porsche, explained the vast bulk of the losses.

The world's second-largest carmaker is battling mounting competition from and falling demand in the core Chinese market.

It is pursuing a major restructuring and downsizing program, trying to bolster falling profit margins, and executives said the difficulties highlighted the urgency of this process.

"The nine-month results make one thing clear: We cannot afford to lose any time. We must act quickly and decisively," chief financial officer Arno Antlitz said in a video statement.

The results were the latest reminder of the pressure on VW — and the wider German and Western automotive industry — to react to increasing competition in China, high costs and practical difficulties moving towards electric car production, and unpredictable and rising tariff burdens, thanks in no small part to US President Donald Trump.

And here are some of the key year-to-date 9-month figures:

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

VW shares were already at their lowest levels in well over 10 years prior to Thursday's announcements, after months of difficult headlines and the ongoing plans to shed tens of thousands of jobs and reduce production capacities.

Perhaps as a result of this, the stock dipped briefly as markets opened and the news was published, but then started to rally as the day progressed.

By midday in Frankfurt, VW shares had climbed by 2% compared to their prices at the start of trading on the DAX.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

CEO Oliver Blume plans to shed around 100,000 jobs across the group, which includes the Audi and Porsche brands, in the coming years though a combination of layoffs and not replacing departing or retiring personnel.

Multiple factors are contributing to this. They include increased competition from Chinese manufacturers, falling revenues in China, changeable US auto tariffs under President Donald Trump, different staffing requirements when manufacturing electric cars and difficulties moving towards making and selling more electric cars at the pace once designated by political leaders.

Up to four plants in Germany could face closure as part of the plan, which has met with considerable union resistance and could lead to strikes starting next year.

CFO Antlitz said the figures showed the urgency underlying these plans, saying the company needed to increase its profit margins by 2030 to solidify its finances.

Antlitz said the operating return on sales was only 3.8% in the first nine months of the year, even before the one-off writedowns hitting the bottom line.

"That is not enough in the long term," he said.

As part of its restructuring program, the VW Group aims to restore an operating profit margin of between 8-10% by 2030.

This year, amid one-off costs now totaling in the region of €10 billion, it expects a profit margin of no more than 1%, compared to prior forecasts in the region of 5%.

#882. Defeat for London City - but is Europe a real possibility?

Clinical Man City edge past London City in WSL thriller

It shows how quickly London City Lionesses have progressed that they were hugely disappointed with a narrow defeat by defending champions Manchester City.

For a team that were playing second-tier football 18 months ago, their lofty ambitions of qualifying for the Champions League suddenly don't seem far-fetched.

London City looked like the better team for most of the afternoon at Hayes Lane but were given a harsh lesson by the visitors in how to be ruthless.

Manchester City needed goals from Khadija Shaw and Lauren Hemp against the run of play, but they dug in to win 2-1 and to continue setting the pace at the top of the Women's Super League.

Those goals came after countless opportunities went begging for London City, who ended the game having had 24 shots but only six on target.

The performance was enough, however, to show that London City are more than capable of competing with the WSL's elite.

The next question is whether they can do it consistently.

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

London City Lionesses are a club who do things differently and, backed by US billionaire Michele Kang, they are not shy to disrupt the current order.

They are an independent women's football club who have spent big in the transfer window and agreed a record-breaking shirt deal with Nike believed to be worth more than Â£3m a year.

They have built their own training facility in Kent and persuaded superstars such as Alexia Putellas to join in the summer.

Spain international Putellas showcased her latest Ballon d'Or trophy - the third of her career - before kick-off on Sunday.

London City Lionesses are clearly no minnows, but even a squad full of superstars needs time to gel.

It was for this reason that people doubted whether they were ready this season to qualify for the Champions League and break the WSL's traditional top three.

But on Sunday's showing, they are not as far off as people thought.

Manager Eder Maestre said the team's performances are already at the level they want but results have not always shown that and they still have work to do.

"That's why it's a very frustrating situation. We were speaking a lot about respecting the identity and it doesn't matter the team that we were facing," the Spaniard said.

"The next step in that project was showing everybody that we can perform, while respecting that identity that we are trying to build on.

"That's why it's doubly frustrating, because I think the result was not the one we deserve. Manchester City are more mature.

"They are more used to it. When you have this consistency and you are very used to playing these kinds of games, maybe you have more experience.

"That's why we have extra nervousness in the moments that we need to be more clinical."

Where London City fell was where Manchester City stood tall.

Moments of brilliance by world-class players Shaw and Hemp delivered the goods and when London City's pressure grew, so too did Manchester City's resilience.

It is that consistency across 90 minutes, and the season as a whole, that Manchester City manager Andree Jeglertz believes will demonstrate the difference.

"They are a very good team and they really showed the highest level," said Jeglertz.

"What it means to be at the top of this league, is playing week after week, and at the same level - and finding different levels to win.

"That is what we have created. That's what everybody who wants to win something needs to be able to do. To contest, you need to compete for the whole season."

London City Lionesses dominated the first half as shown by the momentum swings

London City Lionesses are providing plenty of optimism on the pitch, but even if they were to qualify for the Champions League this season, are they allowed to?

Current Uefa rules state that owners cannot have two clubs competing in the same competition, meaning one of Kang's Lyon or London City Lionesses would potentially miss out.

It is a dilemma that many have discussed, but if they continue to perform so well, it could prove to be a problem earlier than expected.

"First of all, what we feel is important, is to be part of the conversation," London City's chief executive officer Martin Semmens told BBC Sport.

"The next stage is getting towards trophies. Our ambition is to be in Europe, to play in Europe every year, and to compete with the likes of Barcelona and Arsenal.

"We're probably one step behind that in squad development and all the other things we have to do. But on our day, we feel we can beat them."

London City's ambitions are clear - so what happens if they do qualify this season?

"I think Michele [Kang] has a really clear view and that is that she wants to see as much investment come into the women's game as possible," added Semmens.

"The men's multi-club ownership rules is about being careful not to have control over two clubs. We see it differently on the women's side.

"We want to see more investment, so we believe if you invest in more than one club, the game will accelerate faster.

"We truly understand and respect the rules, always. But there are logical, structured ways that we can compete in Europe next season."

#881. Shaw among big names to miss out on FifPro World XI

Manchester City stars Khadija Shaw (left) and Lauren Hemp (right) missed out

Eyebrows were raised on Monday when the FifPro Women's World XI shortlist was unveiled and several big names were missing.

The 26-player shortlist was voted for by players from around the world and is the only award decided solely by fellow footballers.

It is considered prestigious as a result but when the list dropped and five of the top 10 Ballon d'Or finishers were not included, it understandably caused a stir.

Among the notable absentees was Manchester City's top scorer Khadija Shaw, who finished third in the Ballon d'Or.

Malawi star Temwa Chawinga and Haiti's Melchie Dumornay were also shock omissions, along with Barcelona's Caroline Graham Hansen and Denmark captain Pernille Harder.

However, England trio Ella Toone, Chloe Kelly and Aggie Beever-Jones are surprise inclusions.

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

The world XI shortlist was voted for by 6,511 women's footballers from 64 countries via an online system with FifPro.

The finalists are the players who received the most votes judged on their period between 4 August 2025 and 16 August 2026.

All players had to feature at least 20 times during that period to be eligible for nomination and the winners will be unveiled on Monday, 9 November (13:00 GMT).

The world XI will consist of one goalkeeper, three defenders, three midfielders and three forwards who all received the most votes in their positions.

The remaining spot will be taken by the outfield player, from any position, with the next highest number of votes.

Votes for a player in more than one position (for example, if they are named as a midfielder or a forward), are combined.

It is not the first time the shortlists have been controversial.

Last year, Arsenal and Spain midfielder Mariona Caldentey was not included in the FifPro World XI despite coming runner-up in the Ballon d'Or.

In 2024, when 7,000 women's footballers voted, four of the top five in the Ballon d'Or were not shortlisted, including the often overlooked Graham Hansen.

Instead, five Lionesses made the cut despite not winning a major trophy that year or having any finalists in the Ballon d'Or top 10.

This time around the WSL's Player of the Year Shaw missed out. She helped Manchester City win a league and FA Cup double as their top scorer with 21 goals in 22 games.

Meanwhile, the inclusions of England trio Toone, Kelly and Beever-Jones were controversial with all three initially failing to make the most recent Lionesses squad.

Chelsea's Beever-Jones scored just seven goals in all competitions for club and country during the period of voting, while Toone and Kelly both struggled for form and fitness in that time.

In contrast, England team-mates Lauren Hemp of Manchester City and Chelsea's Lauren James were in good form and impressed for their clubs but missed out.

However, Lyon striker Ada Hegerberg is in. The 2018 Ballon d'Or winner did not score in the knockout stages of the Women's Champions League and was not a guaranteed starter for Lyon in the first period of voting in what was a below-par season for her standards.

Goalkeepers: Ann-Katrin Berger (Gotham, Germany), Catalina Coll (Barcelona, Spain), Hannah Hampton (Chelsea, England).

Defenders: Ona Batlle (Barcelona/Arsenal, Spain), Lucy Bronze (Chelsea, England), Ellie Carpenter (Chelsea, Australia), Emily Fox (Arsenal, USA), Alex Greenwood (Manchester City, England), Mapi Leon (Barcelona/London City Lionesses, Spain), Katie McCabe (Arsenal/Chelsea, Republic of Ireland), Irene Paredes (Barcelona). Spain)

Midfielders: Aitana Bonmati (Barcelona, Spain), Ghizlane Chebbak (Al-Hilal/Free Agent, Morocco), Patri Guijarro (Barcelona, Spain), Anaele Le Moguedec (Paris FC, France), Vicky Lopez (Barcelona, Spain), Alexia Putellas (Barcelona/London City Lionesses, Spain), Ella Toone (Manchester United, England).

Forwards: Barbra Banda (Orlando Pride, Zambia), Aggie Beever-Jones (Chelsea, England), Athenea del Castillo (Real Madrid, Spain), Ada Hegerberg (OL Lyonnes, Norway), Chloe Kelly (Arsenal, England), Ewa Pajor (Barcelona, Poland), Claudia Pina (Barcelona, Spain), Alessia Russo (Arsenal, England).

#880. Cristiano Ronaldo merely the latest example of a great player who couldn’t let go | Jonathan Wilson

There is no doubt his international career was an incredible one, but it would have been greater still if he had not lingered on the stage so long

Nothing, perhaps, is quite so difficult for an elite sportsperson as timing their exit. It’s not easy for any person in any job to weigh the hope of having more to give with the desire not to linger beyond their usefulness, but it’s perhaps particularly hard for top athletes because unrealistic self-confidence is so essential to their success. It takes an almost unhealthy level of self-belief for anybody to make the sacrifices to get to the top, to dedicate themselves to such a precarious vocation, to overcome all the setbacks and injuries and failures. How can someone – whose whole life has been spent assuring themselves there are no odds they cannot overcome – accept that is it, that the time has come to say goodbye?

The news that Cristiano Ronaldo has retired from international football brings with it, inevitably, a sadness. Sadness we will no longer see him skipping past a defender, or burying a neck-thrusting header, and sadness in that the end of the career of any great is a reminder of mortality; all things in time must pass. But there is also a sadness he timed his departure so badly. For at least three tournaments, there has been a sense of Ronaldo holding Portugal back.

At the 2022 World Cup, Fernando Santos belatedly took the decision to leave Ronaldo out for the last-16 tie against Switzerland. Portugal suddenly had a fluency and fluidity they had lacked for years and the player who had replaced Ronaldo, Gonçalo Ramos, scored a hat-trick. That seemed incontrovertible evidence the end was upon Ronaldo, or at least his role might become that of an impact substitute.

But even in the final minutes of that game, half the crowd were chanting for Ronaldo. Some, perhaps, were Portuguese fans but many were tourists. They didn’t care much about the result or who went through, they just wanted to see the famous man do the famous thing. Near the end, he scored a goal that was obviously offside. He knew it was offside, but he also knew what his public wanted. So he did the “Siuuuu …” celebration and was rewarded with the biggest cheer of the night. This was like seeing late-period Elvis in Las Vegas: it didn’t matter he was no longer the singer he had been, he was still Elvis. It’s just that Elvis wasn’t also carrying Portugal’s World Cup hopes on his rhinestoned shoulders.

When a player has such celebrity status, when he is still somehow the show no matter how sluggish his movements, making that decision on when to quit must become even harder. And Ronaldo, with his status as Portugal’s greatest soft-power export, also became a political issue. A cabinet minister publicly said he couldn’t be dropped because of how much revenue he generated and what he meant for Portugal’s brand. Portugal is not a country replete with global superstars.

Portuguese Football Federation "Every drop of sweat, every decisive goal, and every captain’s arm-band he wore with honour on the field reflected his unconditional love ⁠for our jersey. His dedication ⁠and his legacy ​transcend the four lines of the field. Ronaldo has raised Portugal’s profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for ⁠many of us, he is the greatest player of all time! …"

Al-Nassr (Ronaldo's current club) "It’s not just a chapter – it’s history you’ve shaped. You’re an icon to the entire world, not ⁠just Portugal. Portugal is in your heart, and you are in the hearts of the world. A page ​has turned, but there is still history left ‌for us to write together at ‌your home, Al-Nassr."

Manchester United (one of Ronaldo's former clubs) "Congratulations on an incredible international career."

Bruno Fernandes (Portugal and Manchester United) "Thank ‌you for the inspiration. It was a privilege to be able to share great moments with our national team alongside my childhood idol."

Diogo Dalot (Portugal and Manchester United) "They don’t know that dreams are a constant in life … Portugal’s history tells us that we are a people who have never accepted limits, unafraid of uncharted seas or weathering storms. We were and are shaped by achievements, sacrifices, tears, and sweat … ‌By dreams that seem impossible – until someone has the courage to make them a reality. You did it. You made us believe, dream, and achieve! A legacy that will be remembered ​not only for the trophies or the goals, but also for the path you paved for all those who came after you. Your passion and determination to represent our country is something I’ll never forget and that will stay with me forever. I’m immensely proud of everything you’ve done for our national team! Thank you, idol."

Pepe (Former Portugal and Real Madrid defender) "It was more than just soccer. Thanks for everything, Cris."

Gianni Infantino, Fifa president "Few players have ever ​touched the heart of football fans ​around the world quite like Cristiano. A career defined by extraordinary talent, relentless determination and ​an unwavering desire to ‌push the boundaries ​of what is possible … Cristiano has ​achieved milestones that may never be matched but his greatest legacy goes far beyond records, trophies and goals … Thank you, Cristiano, for the passion, the unforgettable moments and the immense contribution you have made to our beautiful game proudly wearing the 'Selecao' shirt. Your international career will forever be part of football’s history." Reuters

Ronaldo hung around at Euro 2024, weeping after missing a penalty against Slovenia, the magnitude of his fame and ego warping perception so everything became about him, no matter how many other hugely gifted players were in that squad. And implausibly he was still doing it at the World Cup this summer: gumming the mechanisms, constantly demanding the ball, occasionally drifting out to the left to get in Rafael Leão’s way. At one point against Spain in what turns out to have been his final World Cup game, Ronaldo was released on the break but, lacking pace, ended up having to turn back and play the ball to his full-back, the opportunity gone. There was something almost painful about seeing a player once so explosive reduced to this.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

There needed to be some sort of intervention. This generation of Portuguese players, who really should be challenging for major honours and not just the Nations League, could not continue to struggle on with such an albatross around their necks. It came from Jorge Jesus, the admirably forthright 72-year-old national coach, who was appointed after the World Cup. He didn’t bring Ronaldo off the bench in the second half of a tight game Portugal ended up winning against Norway. Ronaldo insisted he had been promised minutes – but even if there had been an agreement, it would be absurd to refuse a coach the capacity to adapt to circumstance – and stormed out of the camp, an indication perhaps of how his self-regard had come to distort his judgment.

And, assuming this retirement isn’t some sort of power play to force Jesus out, that is where it ended, with a €255 (£212) fine and 30-day ban over a period in which Portugal had no games. Ronaldo will go back to the Saudi Pro League to continue his pursuit of a 1,000th goal. He has been an extraordinary player. He will be remembered as an all-time great, vying with Eusébio as the greatest Portugal player of all time, but his legacy is undoubtedly tainted by this protracted farewell, by the sense that a player who at his best could win games single-handed, came by the end to be a burden to his national team. His has been a great career, but it would have been greater had it been a little shorter.

#879. Lionesses to face France and Portugal in Nations League

All the Uefa Nations League ties will be played over two legs

England have been drawn to face France, Austria and Portugal in next year's Women's Nations League.

In Nyon, Switzerland, Sarina Wiegman's side were drawn alongside familiar opponents, having faced Portugal in the previous Nations League campaign, while France and Austria have both been recent rivals in major tournament qualifying campaigns.

The Lionesses will begin their campaign in Group A2 across three international windows in February-March, April and June 2027, with each team playing home and away fixtures.

"[France are] a world-class team," said Wiegman. "They have so much quality, they have power, they have technique and they have some players, of course, also playing in the WSL [Women's Super League] and at other top clubs.

"So it's exciting to play them because you will be challenged in the highest possible way and that's what makes us better.

"We played Portugal before the last Euros, when we tied with them away and at home we beat them.

"They're a team who can change their style from playing a possession game to being a little more direct, and they have some players that bring lots of quality on the pitch, but are also powerful in duels."

Now in its third edition, the Nations League also forms part of the qualification pathway for the 2028 Olympic Games and Euro 2029.

The four League A group winners will progress to the semi-finals in October 2027, before the final is played to decide the Nations League champions.

Scotland will face Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden, while the Republic of Ireland were drawn against Spain, Norway and Switzerland.

Wales will play Denmark, Italy and Iceland while Northern Ireland, in Group B3, will play Poland, Finland and Belarus.

Fixture dates and venues will be confirmed in due course.

#878. Castle Cove chases the repeat bid in the November Handicap

In today’s feature, Castle Cove returns from a year off to make it back-to-back successes in an ultra-competitive edition of the November Handicap at Doncaster. We also have competitive action from Southwell and Uttoxeter, live on Sky Sports Racing from 11.55am

We have a busy day’s racing on Saturday with action from Doncaster, Southwell and Uttoxeter, live on Sky Sports Racing...

A typically competitive Virgin Bet November Handicap sees last year's winner Castle Cove and ante-post favourite Nobody Knows headline a field of 23.

William Haggas' Castle Cove has not been seen since landing this pot under Jason Hart last season and rates a fascinating runner under new pilot Cieren Fallon. Up eight pounds from last year's ready success, he must be considered if fit enough on this return.

Nobody Knows has been at the head of the betting for this contest since Monday and Richard Hughes has booked the services of Ryan Moore. The three-year-old caught the eye when staying on to finish fifth at York last month and is expected to step forward again over this extra yardage.

Stablemates Circus Of Rome and Duraji have each-way claims on the best of their form, while Alfred Wincham is another to note. He won by an eased down eight lengths at York on his last outing and must defy a 13-pound higher mark.

Coul Angel and Montassib feature among a field of 21 sprinters for this Listed Virgin Bet Every Saturday Money Back Wentworth Stakes.

Coul Angel arrives on a hat-trick having scored in handicap company at the Curragh and York the last twice. He is now five pounds higher as he heads into Listed company for the first time.

Montassib has not been successful since winning the Haydock Sprint Cup in 2024 but has not been disgraced this season and was fifth in this race last year.

Others to note include Ed Walker pair Sunday Girl and Midnight Tango, while Irish-raider Unique Journey likes soft ground and has Ryan Moore in the saddle.

I'm The One and Felicitas headline a deep edition of this Listed Virgin Bet Daily Price Boosts Irish EBF Gillies Fillies' Stakes at 2.45pm.

The Ed Walker-trained Felicitas scored on her first two starts before finishing runner-up in the Musidora at York. She has not been beaten far in hot races since and looks an obvious contender down in grade.

I'm The One, one-time Oaks favourite, returned from a break with a narrow second at Southwell and she will be expected to take a big step forward as she reverts to the turf under Sean Levey.

Revoir is worth a mention after her excellent second in Group Three company in Italy, while Ribbon Of Sea has first-time cheekpieces.

2.50am Flemington - Defiantly runs in Group Three Handicap. Dylan Browne McMonagle rides.

4.50am Flemington - Group One Champions Sprint where Tempted and Joliestar feature.

5.30am Flemington - Autumn Glow headlines Group One Champions Mile.

6.10am Flemington - Group One Champions Stakes - Aeliana and Sir Delius clash. Cox Plate hero Cosmic Crusader also declared.

#877. How Carpenter has become Chelsea's surprise star

Ellie Carpenter has played in every WSL game for Chelsea this season

When Chelsea were drawing with Roma at half-time and needed to find a goal from somewhere, Sonia Bompastor opted to bring on a defender instead of a striker.

Some of the head coach's staff questioned her decision - but Bompastor was proven right to trust Ellie Carpenter.

The Australian scored within six minutes as Chelsea went on to win 2-0 and has made a key impact for the Blues on several occasions this season.

"I made the final decision and someone in my technical staff said: 'But we need to score, and you are bringing on a defensive player?'" said Bompastor.

"We laughed after the game because I said: 'Right now, she's scoring a lot of goals, so I don't know if she's a more defensive or attacking player!'

"It worked so it's good. I was confident Ellie would create a lot in the second half."

So why has Carpenter been so effective for Chelsea this season?

Watch Carpenter score as Chelsea thrash Charlton 6-0 in the WSL

Unbeaten Chelsea are top of the Women's Super League table, having only dropped points in their opening weekend draw with Aston Villa.

Carpenter has started all but one of their WSL matches and has netted four goals from a full-back or wing-back position.

In Sunday's 6-0 win at Charlton, Carpenter scored in the 13th minute, won the most tackles (three) and made the most ball recoveries (12) of any Chelsea player.

Only Khadija Shaw, Lauren Hemp and Victoria Pelova have had more touches in the opposition box than Carpenter's 56 this season.

And only Manchester City winger Hemp and Tottenham's Drew Spence have created more chances from open play in the WSL than Carpenter.

"She has been brilliant this season and she has that attacking prowess," former England striker Ellen White said on the Women's Football Weekly podcast.

"She has comfort behind her because she has trust in the other defenders and midfielders to give her the licence to go forward.

"I love her celebrations too! Opposition [teams] target players who are most prolific, but Chelsea have four or five who can score from anywhere on the pitch."

Carpenter arrived from Lyon in 2025 where she had worked with Chelsea boss Bompastor and won the Champions League together in 2022.

She was known to be an attacking full-back, like fellow Blues defender Lucy Bronze, and this season has become accustomed to the right wing-back position.

It has worked for Chelsea with Bronze moving inside as part of a back three and they have conceded just four goals this season, the fewest of any WSL side.

Carpenter's success at the other end of the pitch has been clear, but she has not reneged on her defensive duties - ranking second in the squad for successful tackles made.

Ellie Carpenter ranks first at Chelsea this season for touches in the opposition box and for successful passes in the final third

Carpenter has always been a threat for Chelsea, but in her first season in the WSL a regular criticism was that she could be wasteful with her crosses.

That is something Bompastor thinks the 26-year-old has improved on and means she is contributing to more goals - scoring four and assisting one.

The Australian has also created 19 chances in the WSL this season and has played 141 successful passes in the final third, the most by any Chelsea player.

"Ellie is performing at a really good level. She has goals from her left foot too which is unusual," said Frenchwoman Bompastor.

"She is able to impact the game. The way we want to play as a team, she is really important out of possession and in possession.

"In possession, she always has the mindset and mentality to go forward. She has a lot of pace and is improving a lot in terms of her technical aspects.

"She is now able to deliver really good crosses, to be in the box and be clinical to score goals. I'm not sure she can have a bigger impact than what she is right now."

#876. More than 60 flights in 11 months and away games in the Arctic Circle

Laura Kaminski guided Crystal Palace to the WSL 2 title in 2024

When English manager Laura Kaminski was approached to become the head coach of Norwegian club SK Brann in January, she could not turn it down.

She jumped at the opportunity to move abroad and develop her coaching skills and is even competing for a place in the Europa Cup quarter-finals next Wednesday.

It was a decision that paid off as 10 months later, she is celebrating a Norwegian league and cup double after a dream debut season.

"My time in the city [of Bergen] has been brilliant," the 38-year-old told BBC Sport.

"I can't go to the supermarket at the minute because so many people are stopping me to wish me congratulations, which is so nice.

"I'm over the moon and it was nice to get the title done before the last game so we can relax. I thought it was going to go right to the wire.

"It's been a competitive year. I've enjoyed every minute. We had a great night with all our fans, who were waiting for us to return from Oslo."

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

Kaminski on the challenges for English coaches in WSL

Kaminski described it as a "hectic" year as she moved from London to Norway and away from her family to take on the Brann job.

The Englishwoman had spent over a year at Crystal Palace, where she led them to promotion to the Women's Super League in 2024.

She was sacked in February 2025 after a tough WSL season as Palace struggled to compete with better financially-backed clubs.

However, she is regarded as one of the country's brightest female managers and has added to her CV with her experiences in Norway.

"I've learned a lot. It's been chaotic - I counted that I have taken 65 flights in 11 months - so it's been exhausting, but what an experience!" added Kaminski.

"To go all the way up to the Arctic Circle and play away [games] in freezing cold conditions with horizontal snow, to beautiful days in Bergen.

"Palace was totally different to Brann. I'm at a club that expects to win the Toppserien [the Norwegian top-flight] as they believe they have invested the most.

"That's been a real challenge. The WSL is dominated by the favourites in the pack so it wasn't always the expectation to get three points against big teams [at Palace]."

Kaminski admits being away from loved ones is "hard" and she has had to be prepared to "make sacrifices" but Brann's trophy success makes it worth it.

She has also picked up new ideas for her coaching philosophy having experienced the high-risk, attack-minded football in Norway.

"Norwegian teams are almost guaranteed to concede every game because they play such attacking football with no fear, and a relentlessness to press," she added.

"That is a bit different to what I was used to. When I watched the tactical displays when I first came in, I was a little bit alarmed at what people were doing.

"But when you play against their sides, and against that [pressing], it is really difficult. It's given me a lot of fuel for the future.

"There are some really fit, fast and athletic players here. It's not a surprise that big, big clubs are coming in for them."

Laura Kaminski spent a year and a half at Crystal Palace

After a season in Norway, Kaminski believes she is a better coach.

She had spent over 15 years as an assistant manager at various clubs in the WSL 2 and WSL and a coaching role with England's under-19s before joining Palace.

But having added European experience to her CV, Kaminski hopes it will open the door to more opportunities in the future.

"I'd like to think I've got a well-rounded skillset to be able to manage at the top level. Right now, my focus is on Brann and a new chapter," said Kaminski.

"There's only two levels in England that are professional. I definitely wanted to get European exposure, which I was never going to get in England.

"At the time, I was in discussions with a few clubs but it was things that I'd done before, or the project wasn't matching.

"I knew that when I came to Brann, I was going to coach top-level players. I wanted to be at the top of the competition and I was desperate to win a trophy."

Kaminski has urged other female coaches in England to go abroad and gain experience as she believes opportunities are too few in the WSL.

A study from UK Coaching in October showed there has been a 6% decline in the overall number of female coaches in recent years.

There are currently three English female coaches in the WSL - Jo Potter at Crystal Palace, Amy Merricks at Birmingham City and Karen Hills at Charlton Athletic - and they all came up with promoted clubs this summer.

But Kaminski says she is "concerned" about where they might go next and hopes more opportunities in English men's football will open up soon.

"I ended up leaving the country to go and get what I thought I deserved and had earned the right to work in, in terms of the level," said Kaminski.

"There's more than one female out there that's capable [of working in men's football]. I don't think it's out of reach. I would always, certainly, be open to it.

"At the moment, for me, there's not enough consideration even for that opportunity to be given to female managers who are more than capable.

"I think the foundations are there for females to take the plunge but is the world of football ready? I'm unsure."

Money, family and sexism - why the number of women coaches is dropping

#875. NWSL playoff predictions: who can spoil Gotham’s bid for the double?

Our panel breaks down the players to watch, the dark horses, the state of the league and the top candidates to reach the championship game in DC

Compelling storylines that kept the league interesting during a crowded sports summer. The interval years that aren’t Olympic or World Cup years are often quieter for the NWSL (see: average attendance was essentially flat among the non-expansion teams). In a year with the men’s World Cup on home soil and a major anniversary season for the WNBA, most of the NWSL’s teams gave a solid showing, with close competition for the Shield, an entertaining Golden Boot race and the returns of several big stars. Even those teams who did not give a solid showing – hello, Chicago – finally made some encouraging moves in the right direction. (Louisville next, please.) Ella Brockway

The league working to gauge the heart of its fanbase. Recent weeks have seen contentious scenes, especially in Portland, as transphobic organizations try to work into the league discourse as they have with the WNBA. But beyond that, there have been considerable innovations made with an eye on garnering more attention. The “Rodman Rule” was hurried to production in part to keep arguably the most marketable US player from going abroad. The league briefly considered following MLS’s lead and inverting its schedule, only for a vote to be spurned after initial backlash from players and the public. It even got a feature in Ted Lasso. These efforts take time, but that’s a lot of willingness to change just about anything about the league’s structure if it moves the needle. Jeff Rueter

Races to the top – and the bottom. The competition for both the Shield and Golden Boot was fierce. Ashley Sanchez pulled ahead for the Boot, but Barbra Banda, Sophia Wilson, Janine Sonis and Trinity Rodman provided some real fireworks. (Had Banda not been kept out of the country for the last month of games due to federal travel policies, she may have given Sanchez a run for her money.) The Shield race was even tighter, with three teams still in contention with two matches to go. However, the league struggled to maintain that quality across the board. Chicago, Louisville and Bay FC were embarrassingly bad – and boring – throughout the season. It’s a story that is too familiar, and doesn’t seem poised to change in a real way any time soon. As much as the league’s marketing centers parity, its choices prioritize expansion. With two new clubs arriving in 2028 and more on the way after, I worry the talent across the board will continue to be watered down, especially as the league’s salary cap and low minimum salary drives elite players away to teams in Europe, Mexico and Brazil. The NWSL will have to contend with what growing pains are inevitable, and which should really be avoided. Abigail Segel

Denver Summit. I’m as disappointed as anyone that we won’t get to see Sanchez’s goalscoring feats continue this postseason, but I’d also like to see what Denver and their goalscorers could have done as just the second expansion franchise to reach the playoffs in their first year. They tied 2018 North Carolina with the third-most goals (53) of a team in any regular season. EB

On talent and in moments, it felt like expansion Denver Summit’s place in the top eight would be inevitable. Ultimately, inconsistency and an inability to turn close games from draws into wins held them back. Only Chicago had a more languid defensive press after the summer break, and while being the league’s lowest-fouling team wins spirit points, it did afford Denver’s opponents plenty of time to build into sequences. JR

For the second year in a row, the North Carolina Courage. The Courage spent most of the season above the playoff line, but when Sanchez’s numbers came back down to earth in the final month, they lacked an attacking structure to keep the goalscoring, which had papered over their leaky defense all year. Mak Lind will look to use his first full offseason to find a sustainable way to make up for Manaka Matsukubo’s absence – her midseason departure to Chelsea did him no favors, and the success they had for almost the entire rest of the season is all the more impressive considering it. AS

Angel City. No team is in better form. After a rough start to the season, Angel City steadied the ship after the summer break and have been blistering of late, with eight wins, two draws and zero losses since 31 August. They have nine goals in their last three, and will have new signing Maddie DiMaria, fresh off a 12-goal showing at the U-17 World Cup, available to face Kansas City. I’d fear them. EB

For once, Gotham don’t qualify. Since selling Alyssa Thompson to Chelsea, Angel City have come out of their doldrums with impressive aptitude. No team has maintained a higher points-per-game rate since 28 August (2.6), and they notched a draw at Gotham and an away win over Washington. Ally Sentnor has made a quick acclimation, and there’s considerable talent including Sveindís Jónsdóttir’s goal threat, Emily Sams’s defensive mettle and Gisele Thompson’s all-around strengths. JR

Angel City. The club whose branding has traditionally been better than its soccer started the season hot, but within a few games they fell back to their expected place in the middle of the table. In June, GM Mark Parsons had seen enough, and gave the boot to manager Alexander Straus. His interim replacement, Leif Smerud, has managed to get the most out of the roster by bringing them back to the basics. Even Sentnor, who did not reach her potential at Utah or Kansas City, has been shining bright after joining midseason. This is a scrappy team peaking at the right time. AS

I know the danger of picking against this team in the playoffs, but I’ll say Gotham. Of any team in this league, they are probably the one with the best plug-and-play system, where players can fill in for others as needed. The question: will they have the healthy bodies to do so? Much depends on the availability of Jaelin Howell, Rose Lavelle and Jaedyn Shaw. EB

I wouldn’t say I necessarily expect any of the top four to falter, but seeding isn’t the only reason I’d lean Kansas City. For a few years now, the Current have been able to outlast the fiercest of challenges thanks to the singular brilliance of Temwa Chawinga on the break, but Angel City’s Sarah Gorden is the rare defender with the backtracking pace to keep in stride with the Malawi international. The Current fare well against teams trying to play out of the back, but Angel City are quite capable at bunkering and countering. I could see them pulling a quick curtain on Chris Armas’s first NWSL postseason. JR

Washington had their best performance of the season on 17 October, defeating rival Gotham for the first time since 2024. It was finally a complete, convincing game from an inconsistent side. But the following game, at Kansas City, was a 2-1 loss made significantly worse by midfield mainstay Hal Hershfelt tearing her ACL. Next was Decision Day against last-place Chicago. Instead of a rout, the Spirit put in a quiet 2-0 win that left little confidence the team is peaking for the playoffs. Washington have reached the last two finals, and it’s possible they will again, but they need to quickly solidify a midfield that’s been fluid all season and will rely heavily on new players Clara Luvanga and Mélissa Bethi to perform as if they know the league inside and out. AS

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

Trinity Rodman. For the first time in two years – I almost want to knock on wood as I’m typing – the Washington Spirit’s star forward enters the NWSL postseason healthy. In 2024, she played every minute of their three playoff games but was battling back issues throughout. In 2025, she was limited to just 35 minutes in three games with an MCL injury. This year, she started all 30 regular-season games and played some of her best soccer (12 goals and eight assists). She’s vital to any Spirit run. EB

If you haven’t yet had the pleasure, make sure to watch Pietra Tordin. The Portland Thorns playmaker has been electric in her second season, settling in as a tricky attacking midfielder with plenty of tricks to thwart anyone marking her one-v-one. Her partnership with Wilson will keep Washington from getting too comfortable, and she’s absolutely one to watch for the USWNT in the short and long term after debuting for Emma Hayes in October. JR

The Current have perhaps the most exciting roster of attackers in the league. Chawinga, Michelle Cooper, Debinha and Haley Hopkins are a formidable bunch. Yet the mastermind behind them is who makes everything tick. Croix Bethune remains the most fun player to watch in the league, constantly connecting teammates and creating chances out of thin air. Bethune was out with an injury earlier this fall but has come back without missing a beat, including earning an assist against her former Washington team two weeks ago. If Bethune continues her MVP-caliber season, there’s nothing Kansas City can’t do. AS

San Diego 2-1 Angel City. An all-west coast matchup for an east coast final. Angel City have a win and a draw with Kansas City this season (albeit the latter result was against a shorthanded Current team). They’re good at pulling off surprises, and I can see a run to the final in DC. The Wave fell just short of the Shield, but they’ve done an excellent job assembling talent across the experience range, from rookie-of-the-year favorite Mimi Van Zanten to 23-year-old Trinity Byars to Kenza Dali, a sneaky MVP candidate at 35. They have the blend to take home the championship. EB

Gotham 2-1 San Diego. While high-flying attacks win hearts and minds, a dependable defense is an invaluable floor-raiser. Gotham won their first Shield thanks to establishing greater control in matches, but their low goalscoring record suggests there’s more to tap into in the final third. I back the collective brilliance of Lavelle, Shaw and Sam Kerr to step up as they so often do in the big moments. JR

San Diego 2-1 Angel City. The bracket feels awfully lopsided this year. The winner of Kansas City v Angel City will probably face off against Gotham in New Jersey for the semi-finals (assuming the Shield winners defeat eighth-place Seattle). Gotham are postseason monsters, as evidenced in 2023 and 2025, but without the injured Howell and Jordynn Dudley, they look a lot less sturdy and a lot less threatening. (Keeper Ann-Katrin Berger, however, can negate a multitude of sins.) The winner of this semi-final is a toss-up between the three, but I’ll go with Angel City for the sake of chaos. On the other side of the bracket, San Diego are peaking while Washington, Portland and Utah are much less convincing. The Wave have nearly perfected their possession-based style with an extremely balanced and consistent lineup. I don’t see a better team right now. AS

#874. The surprising reason women in academia do more parenting than men

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Rachel Fieldhouse is a reporter for Nature in Sydney, Australia.

Flexible working conditions often mean mothers in academia do more parenting than men. Credit: Jelena Cvetkovic/Alamy

Flexible working policies at universities that are designed to make work life easier for parents and carers can reinforce gendered parenting roles, according to a growing body of research published this year. For instance, when workplaces offer flexibility, women end up taking on a greater share of parenting than men.

Universities “have all these policies in place, and we see so many women in science,” that many people assume that women can participate in work as much as men, says Cassidy Sugimoto, an information scientist at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. But “the problem is being solved with women carrying an extraordinary burden”.

Research has already established that parenthood has a greater impact on the careers of female academics than those of men. Sugimoto and her colleagues wanted to find out how much parenting academics do, and how that affects their productivity.

They surveyed more than 10,000 parent academics with academic or non-academic partners at universities and research organizations globally1. They found that women in academia were more likely to be the lead parent and do most of the parenting. Even when women shared parenting or took a secondary role, what the authors call satellite parenting, women ended up doing more than men did when they were the satellite parent. The only task that men were consistently doing more than women was coaching their child’s sports team, says survey co-author Gemma Derrick, a meta-researcher at the University of Bristol, UK.

The team then wanted to understand why women in academia were doing more parenting. Sugimoto and her colleagues found that women used flexible working policies — such as being able to adjust their hours to work earlier or later in the day — to take on more parenting responsibilities2. In academic couples, men, however, used the option of flexibility to justify why they did not do as much parenting as their female partner. For example, some men said that their partner chose to have a more flexible career to look after children.

A female academic from the United Kingdom wrote in the survey that work flexibility meant it was easy for their partner to rely on them “always being available” to help with the kids. Another academic from the United States said: “I have the flexibility to drop off, pick up kids, send them for all activities, and feed them. I have the flexibility to make up all the work time I give up during daytime at night, work till 2am or at least midnight.”

Sanjee Perera, a workforce researcher at the Adelaide University, Australia, says academia has the “illusion of flexibility” because researchers have more autonomy to fit work around parenting responsibilities. But researchers are expected to publish papers, secure external funding, supervise students, teach and attend conferences, she says. “It’s almost like an open-ended workload.”

When men in academia attempted to use flexible working to parent more, they often faced belittling comments or impacts on their careers, says Derrick. The perception of parenting as a gendered responsibility is changing over time, she says. “The question is whether it’s changing fast enough,” she adds.

Another survey3 of 26 female academics in the United Kingdom, by Guoxin Ma, a workplace equity researcher at the Royal Agricultural University in Cirencester, UK, and their colleagues reported that flexible workplace policies, such as working from home or having adjustable working hours, made it harder for women to progress their careers after having children.

Some respondents said that they were seen as less committed to work because they worked from home, finished early or were part-time, while others said that they continued working while on leave because there was no one else to do their work.

Parenting became more equal in many households during the COVID-19 pandemic, says Sugimoto. Some couples looked after their children on alternating days or in ‘shifts’, particularly if one parent had fixed working hours. Flexible working arrangements existed before the pandemic, but now ‘hybrid working’ such as online teaching and meetings has became more normalized4.

#871. Germany seeks new head of state

The question of who should become Germany's new president is becoming pressing. Many want to see Germany's first female head of state. Chancellor Friedrich Merz is keeping his cards close to his chest.

Wanted: A new head of state — female, male, or other. Requirements: German citizen, entitled to vote, minimum age 40. Please apply as soon as possible! Availability starting January 30, 2027; job starts March 19, 2027.

This is not an official job posting, but Germany's federal government is indeed looking for someone to fill the nation's highest office. Having already served two terms, current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is no longer eligible for another, leaving the position open for a successor. Many feel that it is time for Germany's first-ever female head of state.

"The person should have a certain level of public recognition, be politically unbiased, capable of bringing people together, approachable and a reasonably good [public] speaker," political scientist Ursula Münch told DW.

In Germany, a federal parliamentary republic, the president serves as head of state and a representative of the country as well as someone who embodies moral authority for the nation. Unlike in the US, France, or Russia, the president does not wield extensive political power or direct government affairs.

Steinmeier was nominated by his own party, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), in 2009. However, once elected via a convention of parliamentarians and state electors, a president-elect has to suspend their party membership in order to serve in the office apolitically. This time, it is Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democrats (CDU), the senior partner in the coalition government with the SPD and the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), which has the right to nominate a candidate.

Political scientist Münch said that "the three parties must agree on a person who is acceptable for all three." Since the convention that will select Steinmeier's successor is currently controlled by these three parties and their delegates, it is very likely that whomever Merz nominates will be elected.

"Well, I would really like it to be a woman this time. We've had 12 male federal presidents since 1949 — it's about time for a woman. But if the right man were to be nominated, I'd be fine with that too," said Münch. According to an August survey conducted by the Forsa polling institute for the RTL television network, about 74% of German respondents say they don't care whether it's a man or a woman. Another 19% explicitly want a woman, while 5% prefer a man.

Ilse Aigner, president of the Bavarian State Parliament in Munich, appears to have a good chance. Aigner is a member of the smallest party in the coalition, the Bavarian CSU, and is considered a unifying figure. She also has experience in government in Berlin, having served as agricultural minister at the federal level. She enjoys strong support within her Bavarian CSU party, whose leader Markus Söder recently said: "It would be tremendous if she became federal president."

Even members of the opposition Greens and the SPD are full of praise for Aigner's candidacy. "What are we actually waiting for? Surely Ilse Aigner has long since secured a majority across party lines?" asked SPD parliamentary group leader Matthias Miersch recently. However, Merz, who is friends with Aigner, has remained tight-lipped so far — possibly also because Aigner is not a member of Merz's party, but rather of its smaller sister party, the CSU.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other potential successors from the CDU membership have been mentioned: Bundestag President Julia Klöckner, former Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer and Education Minister Karin Prien. Hesse's state premier, Boris Rhein, is also a possible candidate. In recent days, another name has been making the rounds: lawyer Ines Claus, who serves as CDU's parliamentary group leader in Hesse and deputy party chair at the federal level — and is largely unknown.

However, rumors that she would be nominated were swiftly shot down by the chancellor. Sources close to Merz emphasized that he has so far "neither made a decision nor put forward a proposal." There are "a number of suitable" options, sources added.

The president is elected every five years by the Federal Convention, which comprises all 630 members of the Bundestag and an equal number of electors who represent the state parliaments. Among them are also prominent figures from the spheres of culture, science, sports and society. The candidate who receives more than 631 votes goes on to assume office. The governing parties — the CDU/CSU and the SPD — have a combined total of 682 votes, a comfortable majority.

The office of the president is often underestimated as merely a ceremonial role. Yet, as an authority standing above the political parties, this person wields considerable political, legal and moral influence. This is especially true in times of political polarization and international crises. While the president does not govern like a chancellor, he or she represents Germany both at home and abroad.

"From a constitutional perspective, the federal president is enormously important. For example, in a political crisis, he could decide whether it makes more sense to dissolve the Bundestag or to advocate for a minority government," explained political scientist Münch. In addition, he reviews and signs laws proposed by politicians.

The federal chancellor and CDU chairman has an interest in an orderly process, say sources close to the government. The "first milestone" will be the meetings of the CDU Presidium and Executive Board on November 9. Until then, discussions will be held with the state chairpersons of the CDU and the CSU. Sources made it clear that the SPD and the Greens will also be consulted, "since the election of the federal president should have broad support across the democratic spectrum."

That is how political scientist Münch sees it: "I still consider the question open, with a slight edge for CSU candidate Ilse Aigner." But there could still be a real surprise, she added.

This article was originally published in German.

#870. Fifa wants talks over restricting women’s Olympic football to under-23s

IOC open to dialogue and Fifa wants input from others

Fifa concerned about fixture congestion and workload

Fifa wants talks with the International Olympic Committee over restricting the Olympic women’s football tournament to under-23s owing to concerns over fixture congestion and the workload of senior players.

The eligibility criteria for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles has been set, with qualification tournaments having begun in some regions, so no change can be made until Brisbane 2032 at the earliest, but sources at both organisations have said that they are open to dialogue.

Although no formal proposal has been made, Fifa is understood to be interested in examining the matter in talks with the IOC and other key stakeholders, such as the players and leading member associations whose national sides routinely qualify for the Games.

A move to bring in age restrictions would dramatically alter the nature of the event and require careful analysis, consultation and consideration through Fifa and IOC processes.

Such a change would be controversial and could provoke a backlash from leading international players because the Olympics has long been regarded as one of the highlights of the women’s calendar, with Emma Hayes’s United States team securing gold in Paris two years ago. The Olympic title has been contested eight times and the US have won five.

Women’s football also has a major commercial appeal for the IOC, particularly in markets such as the US, Europe and Australia, so it may resist Fifa’s overtures.

Women’s football was introduced to the Olympics at Atlanta in 1996, and as an amateur sport at that time never had eligibility requirements, in contrast to the men’s game.

After admitting football to the Olympic programme in 1908 the IOC did not permit professionals to take part until 1984 owing to Fifa’s insistence on maintaining the primacy of the World Cup, as well as the demands on players from a congested calendar. Under pressure from Fifa the IOC introduced an under-23 age restriction in 1992, although three overage players have also been allowed in each squad since 1996.

The huge growth and professionalisation of the women’s game over the past decade has created increased fixture congestion, with the 2028 calendar the most bloated yet.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Fifa is to a large extent culpable for this because the world governing body has chosen to launch the Women’s Club World Cup in an Olympic year, with the US to stage the 16-team competition between 5 and 30 January, six months before the Games.

The Women’s Club World Cup will cause major disruption to the European club season, with Arsenal and Chelsea or Manchester City likely to be absent from domestic competition for up to a month if they reach the latter stages, missing four Women’s Super League matches and the FA Cup fourth round. The importance of the sport to the IOC is shown by the fact that the women’s football tournament will be bigger than the men’s for the first time in LA, featuring 16 teams to 12, in a reversal of the numbers at Paris 2024.

If someone would've said to me I'd be doing this as a job when I was 12, I wouldn't have believed them.

My name's Jacob. I'm a content creator, and I work with Bolton Wanderers.

My role here at Bolton is coming up with new ideas for social media, to try new concepts, filming stuff, and then posting them onto Bolton's pages and trying to help people follow the club. In my opinion, I think it's one of the funnest jobs in football, and it's brilliant.

Right. Welcome to Bolton, Larra. I hope I said that right. I'm going to teach you some Bolton twang to help you settle in.

My passion for football when I was growing up started at a very young age. My dad used to take me to the football matches, and I got my very first season ticket when I was five years old in the 2010/11 season, when Bolton was in the Premiership. Being something I loved as a kid, to turn it into my job is amazing.

I work here at least two days a week, obviously filming content, producing content,and then on match day, I'll be filming mostly with fans, and I love it.

As a town? Well, for us, it's lovely. Yeah.

Mondays, meetings. We have the marketing meeting, so that gives you an idea of what the week holds, what I'm going to do on a match day with the fans. And then in the week, I either film in with players, retail, commercial,whatever department needs help producing videos.

Some of the skills I use, I think one of them's got to be communication. You've got to be able to talk to people, talk to fans, and if you're watching this and you're a bit shy, or you think you can't communicate with people as well, I was like that inhigh school, so you learn it as you get older. But working in football, you've got to be adaptable because one minute you're doing a new signing, next minute you're working with the players, next minute it's a match day, next minute the season's over.

I'd say another one is being creative. That's probably the most important one because without being creative, you won't be able to put a video together.

So when I was 16 in high school, that's where my journey started. I did videos, which got me a number of followers. I always struggled in the classroom side in high school, but creating content and creating ideas and being creative, I was always really, really good at in high school, whether that would be doing something drama-related or English, writing, creating stories. I always knew I had a passion for creative pieces of work and being able to now do it as a job, it suits me down to the ground.

I think don't wait for an opportunity to come to you. Get out there and try. If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role there. The highlight of my career so far, probably looking back, being resilient enough to create my own career path in doing something I love.

When you score this season, you might be chuffed.

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

He's a content creator for Bolton Wanderers FC, coming up with new ideas for social media, filming videos and posting them onto official pages. The aim is to encourage people to follow the club.

There are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he says. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities."

Jacob says salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

Find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

#868. How to become a football referee

Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and said sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your plan and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

With a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

If you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:

In her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees new referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she says. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared."

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she says. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

As well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful."

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.
